張思〔貫直隸河間府任丘縣，民籍，國子生，治詩經，字慎父，行四，年三十三，九月初九日生〕。曾祖廣，祖政，父軏〔義官〕，母徐氏。慈侍下，兄恩、忠〔己丑進士〕、恕。娶朱氏。順天府鄉試第二十三名，會試第一百三十二名。

傅鎮〔貫福建永寧衛中左千戶所，軍籍，福清縣人，國子生，治詩經，字國鼎，行二，年三十二，正月二十二日生〕。曾祖興，祖福〔壽官〕，父珙，母劉氏。具慶下，兄鎧，弟鏜、鉞。娶陳氏。福建鄉試第十名，會試第三十六名。

馬中驥〔貫四川成都府新都縣，民籍，國子生，治易經，字惟德，行一，年三十八，八月二十二日生〕。曾祖程，祖宗義，父先，母林氏。嚴侍下，弟中龍、中駿、中騄。娶李氏。四川鄉試第三十一名，會試第七十四名。
translation_en:
Lei Li 雷禮 was registered in Fengcheng County, Nanchang Prefecture, Jiangxi, in a civilian household. A National University student specializing in the Book of Odes, he had the courtesy name Bijin and was first in birth order, aged twenty-seven, born on the thirteenth day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Qiyang; his grandfather, Suichong; his father, Bangjian; and his mother, née Zheng. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Di, Xiang, Mi, Zhi, and Yin, and his younger brother was Hu. He married a woman née Li and subsequently a woman née Zhang. He placed twenty-fourth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 109th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Si 張思 was registered in Renqiu County, Hejian Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, in a civilian household. A National University student specializing in the Book of Odes, he had the courtesy name Shenfu and was fourth in birth order, aged thirty-three, born on the ninth day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Guang; his grandfather, Zheng; his father, Yue〔an honorary official recognized for charitable contributions〕; and his mother, née Xu. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were En, Zhong〔a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the jichou year, 1529〕, and Shu. He married a woman née Zhu. He placed twenty-third in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 132nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Fu Zhen 傅鎮 was registered in a military household of the Central Left Battalion of Yongning Guard, Fujian, and was a native of Fuqing County. A National University student specializing in the Book of Odes, he had the courtesy name Guoding and was second in birth order, aged thirty-two, born on the twenty-second day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Xing; his grandfather, Fu〔an honorary official recognized for longevity〕; his father, Gong; and his mother, née Liu. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Kai, and his younger brothers were Tang and Yue. He married a woman née Chen. He placed tenth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and thirty-sixth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ma Zhongji 馬中驥 was registered in Xindu County, Chengdu Prefecture, Sichuan, in a civilian household. A National University student specializing in the Book of Changes, he had the courtesy name Weide and was first in birth order, aged thirty-eight, born on the twenty-second day of the eighth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Cheng; his grandfather, Zongyi; his father, Xian; and his mother, née Lin. His father was living and his mother deceased. His younger brothers were Zhonglong, Zhongjun, and Zhonglu. He married a woman née Li. He placed thirty-first in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and seventy-fourth in the Metropolitan Examination.

程瑶〔貫直隸德州左衛軍籍，山東掖縣人，州學廩生，治詩經，字子彬，行三，年二十二，二月二十一日生〕。曾祖清，祖恕，父賢，母李氏。重慶下，兄瓀、琳，弟瑀、琛，娶吳氏。順天府鄉試第二十五名，會試第二百九十名。

樊深〔貫直隸大同中屯衛軍籍，國子生，治易經，字希淵，行一，年三十，十二月十三日生〕。曾祖謙〔壽官〕，祖賓〔義官〕，父景時〔義官〕，母潘氏。具慶下，弟潛〔生員〕，娶徐氏。順天府鄉試第七名，會試第一百三十三名。
translation_en:
Bi Xuan, registered in a military household in Panyu County, Guangzhou Prefecture, Guangdong, was a native of Jishui County, Jiangxi. An additional student of the county Confucian school, he specialized in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Yanhui; he was third in birth order, aged twenty-three, and born on the twelfth day of the eleventh month. His great-grandfather was Pian, his grandfather Xi, his father Shu, and his mother née Luo. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Chao and Gang, and he was betrothed to a woman née Huang. He placed seventy-third in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and 124th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Bian Cen was registered in an official household in Renqiu County, Hejian Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region. A student of the Imperial University, he specialized in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Wenyue; he was third in birth order, aged thirty, and born on the ninth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather Yong was Right Vice Minister of Justice at Nanjing. His grandfather Yin was a Registrar and received the honorary title of Secretary in the Ministry of Revenue. His father Yi was Left Administration Vice Commissioner in a Provincial Administration Commission, with his salary increased by two grades. His mother, née Xie, received the title of Lady of Peace. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Ying, an Imperial University student, and Song, a tribute scholar; his younger brothers were Jin, Hang—a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the same examination cohort—and Ze. He married a woman née Shi. He placed twenty-sixth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 131st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Cheng Yao, registered in a military household of the Dezhou Left Guard in the directly administered metropolitan region, was a native of Ye County, Shandong. A stipend student of the department Confucian school, he specialized in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Zibin; he was third in birth order, aged twenty-two, and born on the twenty-first day of the second month. His great-grandfather was Qing, his grandfather Shu, his father Xian, and his mother née Li. His parents and grandparents were living. His elder brothers were Ruan and Lin, and his younger brothers Yu and Chen. He married a woman née Wu. He placed twenty-fifth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 290th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Fan Shen was registered in a military household of the Datong Central Garrison Guard in the directly administered metropolitan region. A student of the Imperial University, he specialized in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Xiyuan; he was first in birth order, aged thirty, and born on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather Qian held an honorary official title for longevity; his grandfather Bin and father Jingshi held honorary official titles for philanthropy. His mother was née Pan. Both parents were living. His younger brother Qian was a government student. He married a woman née Xu. He placed seventh in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 133rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Xu Shouyi, courtesy name Zihe, was registered in a civilian household in Qi County, Kaifeng Prefecture, Henan. A student of the National University specializing in the Book of Odes, he ranked second among his brothers and was forty sui old, born on the twenty-fifth day of the intercalary fifth month. His great-grandfather was Zhi, his grandfather Huai, and his father Wei; his mother was née Wang. Both parents were deceased. His elder brother was Yaoxiang, and his younger brothers were Shouzhi, Yaochen, Shouxin, Shouzhong, Shoude, and Shoulian. His wife was née Wu. He placed fifty-fourth in the Henan Provincial Examination and 145th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xia Yingyuan, courtesy name Tiren, was registered in a civilian household in Jingzhou, Hejian Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region. An added-quota student at the department school specializing in the Book of Rites, he ranked first among his brothers and was twenty-seven sui old, born on the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Tong, chief of a River Anchorage Office; his grandfather was Yue, and his father Shang; his mother was née Wang. His parents and grandparents were living. His younger brothers were Qingyuan and Xiangyuan. His wife was née Yao. He placed sixty-second in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 255th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Dakui, courtesy name Bolun, was registered in an official household attached to the Xiangyang Ceremonial Guard Office in Huguang. A student of the National University specializing in the Book of Odes, he ranked first among his brothers and was thirty-four sui old, born on the twelfth day of the second month. His great-grandfather Lin and grandfather Su were both ceremonial guards; his father Long was a student of the National University, and his mother was née Wang. Both parents were living. His younger brother Daxiao was a tribute scholar (gongshi). His wife was née Mo. He placed sixty-second in the Huguang Provincial Examination and sixty-fifth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Liangzhu, courtesy name Quanyu, was registered in a civilian household in Nan'an County, Quanzhou Prefecture, Fujian. A student of the National University specializing in the Book of Changes, he ranked first among his brothers and was thirty-two sui old, born on the fourteenth day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Shangyu, his grandfather Chun, and his father Hai; his mother was née Huang. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Liangji and Liangcai. His wife was née Huang. He placed eightieth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and forty-seventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Min Dan, courtesy name Jingzhou, was registered in a civilian household in Fuliang County, Raozhou Prefecture, Jiangxi. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Documents, he ranked twenty-sixth in family order, was aged thirty-four, and was born on the first day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was You’an, an honorary official for longevity; his grandfather was Yinfang, a Confucian School Professor; his father was Shichao, and his mother was née Wang. His father was living and his mother deceased. His younger brothers were Xu, Zui, Bing, and Liang, and his wife was née Xu. He placed thirty-sixth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 269th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Chuxiu, courtesy name Shunbi, was registered in a civilian household in Nan’an County, Quanzhou Prefecture, Fujian. An additional student of the prefectural Confucian school specializing in the Book of Changes, he ranked first in family order, was aged twenty-nine, and was born on the seventh day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Ying; his grandfather was Shu, an honorary official for righteousness; his father was Le, his mother was née Lai, and his stepmother was née Cai. Both parents were living. His younger brother was Chucai, and his wife was née Xie. He placed fourteenth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 117th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Fang Ren, courtesy name Zhiyi, was registered in a military household in Huanggang County, Huangzhou Prefecture, Huguang. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals, he ranked first in family order, was aged thirty-eight, and was born on the sixteenth day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Jun, his grandfather was Hua, his father was Yong, and his mother was née Peng. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Shi, Zai, Ji, Zuo, and Jie, and his wife was née Zhu. He placed fourth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and ninety-first in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhou Dali, courtesy name Zihe, was registered in a civilian household in Kunshan County, Suzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region. An additional student of the county Confucian school specializing in the Book of Changes, he ranked second in family order, was aged twenty-seven, and was born on the eighth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Ming, his grandfather was Xuan, his father was Shu, and his mother was née Yan. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Dayou, Dazhuang, and Dalun; his younger brothers were Dazhang, Dabin, Dakui, Daqi, Dazong, Dalu, Damo, and Dashao. His wife was née Wang. He placed fifty-second in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 247th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Zhou Fujun, registered in a civilian household in Taicang Subprefecture, Suzhou Prefecture, Zhili, and a native of Kunshan County, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Ziyu; he ranked second in his family and was aged thirty-seven, born on the fifteenth day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yi; his grandfather, Yuanxue, held a seventh-rank prestige title and was posthumously appointed Judicial Director; his father, Zai, was a Subprefect; and his mother was née Wu. His father was deceased and his mother living. His elder brother Fuwu was a provincial graduate (juren) entitled to wear the official cap and girdle. He married a woman née Huang. He placed thirtieth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and seventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

Guo Xiyan, registered in a civilian household in Fengcheng County, Nanchang Prefecture, Jiangxi, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Zhongyu; he ranked first in his family and was aged twenty-four, born on the seventh day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Weixin, his grandfather Jun, his father Jin, and his mother née Lei. His parents and grandparents were living. His younger brothers were Xizeng, Xisi, Ximeng, and Xizhang. He married a woman née Li. He placed fifteenth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and thirty-seventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

Qian Dehong, registered in a civilian household in Yuyao County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, was an attached student of the county school specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Hongfu; he ranked eighth in his family and was aged thirty-seven, born on the twenty-second day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Shizhi, his grandfather Xi, his father Meng, and his mother née Ma. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Dezhong, Dezhao, and Deshu; his younger brothers were Dezhang, Dezhou, and Deke. He married a woman née Zhu. He placed thirty-seventh in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 231st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Ji, registered in a civilian household in Shanyin County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Ruzhong; he ranked fourteenth in his family and was aged thirty-five, born on the sixth day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Kewang; his grandfather, Li, was a District Magistrate, posthumously appointed Investigating Censor; his father, Jing, held the prestige title Grand Master for Constitutional Service and served as Vice Commissioner of a Provincial Surveillance Commission; and his mother, née Lu, was granted the title Lady (ruren). Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Chao, Ting, Guo, Chen, Fu, and Bang. He married a woman née Zhang. He placed fifty-sixth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and eighteenth in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Shi Ji 史際, registered in Liyang County, Yingtian Prefecture, belonged to a civilian household and was a National University student specializing in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Gongfu, he ranked fourth among his brothers, and he was aged thirty-eight, born on the second day of the eighth month. His great-grandfather was Gao; his grandfather, Zuo, was posthumously appointed Supervising Secretary in the Nanjing Office of Scrutiny for Justice; and his father, Hou, was formerly Vice Minister of the Nanjing Court of Imperial Entertainments, promoted in rank to Grand Master for Court Service (chaolie dafu). His father's former wives were Lady Li, posthumously granted the title Lady (ruren), and Lady Zhang; his mother was Lady Wang, and his stepmother was Lady Xu, granted the title Lady (ruren). His parents and a grandparent or grandparents were living. His elder brothers were Yang and Zhi, and his younger brothers were Jie and Long, the latter a National University student. He married Lady Yang. He placed thirteenth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 225th in the Metropolitan Examination.

He En 賀恩, registered in Yizhen County, Yangzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered territory, belonged to a military household and was a county school student specializing in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Junxi, he ranked third among his brothers, and he was aged thirty-seven, born on the tenth day of the eleventh month. His great-grandfather was An, his grandfather Sheng, his father Ang, and his mother Lady Zou. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Jue and Lu, and his younger brothers were Chong and Zuo. He married Lady Yang. He placed 125th in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 214th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yin Yu 尹宇, registered in Nangong County, Jizhou Subprefecture, Zhending Prefecture, in the directly administered territory, belonged to a civilian household and was an added-quota student at the county school, specializing in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Guangfu, he ranked second among his brothers, and he was aged thirty-two, born on the seventeenth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Sheng, his grandfather Quan, his father Fu 付, and his mother Lady Su. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Xian, and his younger brothers were Guan, You, Rong, and Ning. He married Lady Shi. He placed forty-first in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and eighty-third in the Metropolitan Examination.

Hu Yue 胡岳, registered in Poyang County, Raozhou Prefecture, Jiangxi, belonged to a civilian household and was a National University student specializing in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Zonggao, he ranked seventh among his brothers, and he was aged forty-two, born on the twenty-first day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather, Jingshan, was posthumously granted the rank of Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and the office of Right Vice Minister of Justice; his grandfather was Dinghe, his father Fu 富, his mother Lady Chen, and his stepmothers Ladies Li and Lü. His mother was living and his father deceased. His younger brother, Dai, was an Assistant Office Director in the Nanjing Court of Imperial Entertainments. He married Lady Zhuang. He placed fifty-sixth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 191st in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Gu Chong 顧翀 was registered in a civilian household in Cixi County, Ningbo Prefecture, Zhejiang, and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Yujian; he ranked second among his brothers and was thirty-five years old, born on the twenty-third day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather was Xuan; his grandfather was Fu [?—the transcription reads 父]; and his father was Yi. His father's former wife was née Zhang, his mother née Fang, and his stepmother née Luo. His courtesy name was Chaoming; he ranked second among his brothers and was thirty-four years old, born on the third day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Fu; his grandfather was Ao〔an official awaiting selection for appointment〕; and his father was Shen. His mother and stepmother were both née Zhou. His parents and grandparents were living. His elder brother was Ke; his younger brothers were Pu, Xuan, Bo, and Jie. His wife was née Chen. He placed one hundred thirty-fifth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and ninetieth in the Metropolitan Examination.

title: 嘉靖十一年進士登科錄
text:
皇帝制曰朕惟人君
奉
天命以統億兆而為
之主必先之以咸
有樂生俾遂其安
===
欲然後庶幾盡父
母斯民之任為無
愧焉夫民之所安
者所欲者必首之
以衣與食使無衣

translation_en: The Emperor's decree reads: “We consider that the ruler receives Heaven’s mandate to govern the countless multitudes and be their sovereign. He must first ensure that all find joy in living, enabling them to attain security and satisfy their desires. Only then may he hope to fulfill, without cause for shame, his responsibility to act as father and mother to these people. As for what gives the people security and what they desire, clothing and food must come first. If they have no clothing…

title: 嘉靖十一年進士登科錄
text:
無食未免有凍餒
死亡流離困苦之
害夫匪耕則何以
取食弗蠶則何以
資衣斯二者亦王
===
者之所念而憂者
也今也耕者無幾
而食者衆蠶者甚
稀而衣者多又加
以水旱虫蝗之為

translation_en: …and without food, they cannot escape the afflictions of freezing and hunger, death, displacement, and hardship. Without farming, how can food be obtained? Without raising silkworms, how can clothing be supplied? These two matters are also what a ruler keeps in mind and worries about. Now those who farm are few, while those who eat are many; those who raise silkworms are very few, while those who wear clothes are many. Added to this are floods, droughts, insect pests, and locusts causing…

title: 嘉靖十一年進士登科錄
text:
災遊墮冗雜之為
害邊有煙塵内有
盜賊無怪乎民受
其殃而日甚一日
也固本朕不類寡
===
昧所致上不能參
調化機下不能作
興治理實憂而且
愧焉然時有今昔
權有通變不知何

punctuated: 災，遊墮冗雜之為害，邊有煙塵，内有盜賊，無怪乎民受其殃而日甚一日也。固本朕不類寡昧所致，上不能參調化機，下不能作興治理，實憂而且愧焉。然時有今昔，權有通變，不知何
translation_en: …disasters, and the harm caused by idleness and an excess of miscellaneous persons [?]. At the frontiers there is warfare; within the realm there are bandits. No wonder the people suffer these calamities, their plight worsening day by day. This is surely rooted in [?] My unworthiness and limited understanding: above, I cannot assist in harmonizing the workings of cosmic transformation; below, I cannot invigorate good governance. Truly I am both anxious and ashamed. Yet circumstances differ between past and present, and expedient measures must adapt to change. I do not know what…

title: 嘉靖十一年進士登科錄
text:
道可以致雨暘時
若災害不生百姓
足食足衣力乎農
而務乎織順乎道
而歸乎化子諸士
===
明于理識夫時蘊
抱于內而有以資
我者亦既久矣當
直陳所見所知備
述于篇朕親覽焉

punctuated: 道可以致雨暘時若，災害不生，百姓足食足衣，力乎農而務乎織，順乎道而歸乎化？子諸士明于理，識夫時，蘊抱于內而有以資我者，亦既久矣。當直陳所見所知，備述于篇，朕親覽焉。
translation_en: …by what means can rain and sunshine be brought to accord with the seasons, disasters prevented, and the common people provided with sufficient food and clothing, so that they devote their efforts to farming and weaving, follow the Way, and embrace moral transformation? You scholars have long understood principle and discerned the needs of the times, holding within yourselves insights with which to assist me. You should frankly state what you have seen and what you know, setting it forth fully in your essays. I shall read them personally.

text:
臣林大欽
臣對臣智識愚昧學術疎淺不足以奉
大問竊惟
陛下當亨太之交撫盈成之運天下皆已大治四海
皆已無虞而乃拳拳於百姓之未得所為憂是
豈非文王視民如傷之心耶甚大美也然臣之
所懼者
陛下負聰明神智之資秉剛睿明聖之德舉天下之
事無足以難其為者而微臣所計議復不能有
所補益於萬一
===

綏其禄秩然未聞天下之人有曰
天子某日降某策問某事因某策濟某功者是豈策
士之言皆無可適於用者耶抑亦其言或有可
適於用而未暇採之耶是臣之所懼也臣方欲
為根極政要之說明切時務之論而不敢飾為
迂闊空虚無用之文以罔

punctuated:
臣林大欽。

臣對：臣智識愚昧，學術疎淺，不足以奉大問。竊惟陛下當亨太之交，撫盈成之運，天下皆已大治，四海皆已無虞，而乃拳拳於百姓之未得所為憂，是豈非文王視民如傷之心耶？甚大美也。然臣之所懼者，陛下負聰明神智之資，秉剛睿明聖之德，舉天下之事，無足以難其為者，而微臣所計議，復不能有所補益於萬一，陛下豈能以其言為未可盡棄，而有所取之耶？

陛下臨朝策士凡有幾矣，異時莫不光揚其名聲，寵綏其禄秩，然未聞天下之人有曰：「天子某日降某策，問某事，因某策濟某功者。」是豈策士之言皆無可適於用者耶？抑亦其言或有可適於用，而未暇採之耶？是臣之所懼也。臣方欲為根極政要之說，明切時務之論，而不敢飾為迂闊空虚無用之文以罔陛下。陛下若以其言為可信，而不悉去之，試以臣之策付
translation_en:
Your servant, Lin Daqin.

Your servant replies: My understanding is ignorant and my learning shallow; I am unworthy to respond to Your Majesty’s great question. I humbly reflect that Your Majesty presides over an age of prosperity and peace, governing in a time of abundance and accomplished order. All under Heaven is already well governed, and all within the Four Seas is free from anxiety. Yet you remain deeply concerned that the common people have not found their proper place. Is this not the heart of King Wen, who regarded his people as though they were suffering injury? This is a virtue of the highest order. Yet what I fear is this: Your Majesty possesses keen intelligence and divine wisdom, together with firmness, discernment, illumination, and sageliness. Among all the affairs of the realm, none is difficult for you to undertake. If the proposals of your insignificant servant cannot contribute even the slightest benefit, how could Your Majesty consider his words worth retaining at all, and adopt any of them?

How many times has Your Majesty now presided at court to examine candidates with policy questions? On past occasions, you have invariably brought honor to their names and graciously bestowed stipends and ranks upon them. Yet we have never heard anyone in the realm say: “On such-and-such a day the Son of Heaven issued a particular policy question, asking about a particular matter, and through a particular policy essay accomplished a particular result.” Can it be that the words of all those examined were wholly unsuited to practical use? Or were some of their words usable, but there was no time to adopt them? This is what your servant fears. I intend to offer an explanation that gets to the very foundations of essential government, and a discussion that addresses current affairs clearly and directly. I dare not embellish my writing with remote, empty, and useless rhetoric to deceive Your Majesty. If Your Majesty considers my words trustworthy and does not reject them entirely, try entrusting your servant’s policy essay to …

title: 嘉靖十一年進士登科錄
text:
之有司責其可行則臣終始之願畢焉如或言
不適用則臣有瞽愚欺天之罪俯伏以待罪譴
誠所甘心而不辭也臣伏讀
聖策有以見
陛下拳拳於民生凍餒流離為憂以足民衣食為急
此誠至誠惻怛以惠元元之念天下之所願少
須臾無死以待德化之成者然臣謂
陛下誠懷愛民之心而未得足衣食之道誠見百姓
凍餒流離之形而未知百姓凍餒流離之實也
夫
===

足衣食之道未有人主忍見夫民之凍餒流離

…to the responsible authorities, and charge them with putting into effect what is practicable; then your servant’s lifelong wish will be fulfilled. If, however, my words prove unsuitable for use, I shall be guilty of blind ignorance and deceiving Heaven. Prostrate, I shall await punishment and censure, which I would willingly accept without demur.

This is indeed a thought of utmost sincerity and compassion for the common people. All under Heaven wish to escape death a little longer, so that they may await the fulfillment of your transforming virtue. Never has a ruler endured the sight of the people suffering cold, hunger, and displacement without considering how to rescue them. Never has a ruler acted to rescue the people from cold, hunger, and displacement, only for all under Heaven ultimately to remain trapped in these conditions beyond rescue. Now, an ordinary man’s intentions can find expression within his household, and those of a lord of a thousand chariots within his state. Why? text:
阨夷狄盜賊不能困以恒職修而本業固倉廩
實而備禦先也臣聞立國有三計有萬世不易
之計有終歲應辦之計有因時苟且之計萬世
不易之計者大學所謂生之者衆食之者寡為
之者疾用之者舒者也故王制三年耕則有一
年之積例之則九年當有三年之豫其終嵗所
入盖足以自給而三年之畜恒可以預待不虞
如此者所謂天不能災地不能阨夷狄盜賊不
能困臣前所謂王者之政
陛下今日所方切求而欲勵之行者所謂終歳應辦
===
之計者盖生財之道未甚周節財之道未甚盡
一嵗之入僅足以充一嵗之用其平居無事尤
未見其甚敝偶有凶荒盜賊之變則未免厚斂
重取以至於困敗而不能自振若此者盖素備
不修因時權設漢唐宋以下治天下之大率而
非吾
陛下之所以奉天理物而深厚國脉者其所謂因時
苟且之計者盖平時之所以斂散於民者頗無
其度而取民惟畏其不多用財惟畏其不廣方
其無事百姓已不能自給迨其有變則不可復

阨，夷狄盜賊不能困，以恒職修而本業固，倉廩實而備禦先也。臣聞立國有三計：有萬世不易之計，有終歲應辦之計，有因時苟且之計。萬世不易之計者，《大學》所謂「生之者衆，食之者寡，為之者疾，用之者舒」者也。故《王制》三年耕則有一年之積，例之則九年當有三年之豫。其終嵗所入，盖足以自給，而三年之畜，恒可以預待不虞。如此者，所謂天不能災，地不能阨，夷狄盜賊不能困，臣前所謂王者之政，陛下今日所方切求而欲勵之行者。
所謂終歳應辦之計者，盖生財之道未甚周，節財之道未甚盡，一嵗之入僅足以充一嵗之用。其平居無事，尤未見其甚敝；偶有凶荒盜賊之變，則未免厚斂重取，以至於困敗而不能自振。若此者，盖素備不修，因時權設，漢唐宋以下治天下之大率，而非吾陛下之所以奉天理物而深厚國脉者。
其所謂因時苟且之計者，盖平時之所以斂散於民者，頗無其度，而取民惟畏其不多，用財惟畏其不廣。方其無事，百姓已不能自給；迨其有變，則不可復
translation_en:
…constrain them, nor can foreign peoples or bandits bring them to distress, because regular duties are fulfilled and the fundamental occupation is secure, the granaries are full, and defensive preparations are made in advance. Your servant has heard that there are three plans for establishing a state: a plan that remains unchanging for ten thousand generations, a plan for meeting the needs of each year, and a plan of makeshift expedients adapted to the moment. The plan that remains unchanging for ten thousand generations is what the Great Learning describes: “Let those who produce be many and those who consume be few; let production be swift and expenditure gradual.” Thus, according to the Royal Regulations, three years of cultivation yield one year’s reserves; by the same reckoning, nine years should yield three years’ reserves. The income of each full year is sufficient to meet its needs, while the three years’ accumulated stores can always be held in readiness for unforeseen emergencies. This is what is meant by saying that Heaven cannot bring calamity upon them, Earth cannot constrain them, and foreign peoples or bandits cannot bring them to distress. It is the government of a true king, of which your servant spoke earlier, and which Your Majesty now earnestly seeks and wishes diligently to put into practice.
The plan for meeting the needs of each year is one in which the means of producing wealth are not sufficiently comprehensive and the means of conserving it are not fully employed: one year’s income barely suffices for one year’s expenditure. In ordinary, uneventful times, its severe deficiencies are not yet apparent. But should famine or banditry unexpectedly arise, heavy levies and exactions become unavoidable, ultimately bringing distress and ruin from which recovery is impossible. In such a case, regular preparations have been neglected and temporary measures devised as circumstances demand. This has been the general pattern of governing the realm under the Han, Tang, and Song and thereafter; it is not the means by which Your Majesty would serve Heaven, order all things, and deeply strengthen the state’s vitality.
The so-called plan of makeshift expedients adapted to the moment is one in which the ordinary collection of resources from the people and their distribution among them largely lack proper measure. In taking from the people, the sole fear is that too little will be taken; in spending wealth, the sole fear is that expenditure will not be extensive enough. title: 嘉靖十一年進士登科錄
text:
為之計矣此則制國無紀潰亂不時盖昏亂衰
世之政馬盖臣前所謂起於游墮病於冗雜之
弊亦畧有同於是
陛下今所方欲改轍而易海內之觀者臣謂今日游
墮之弊有二冗雜之弊有三此天下之所以長
坐於困乏而志士至今憤惋而嘆息者也其所
謂游墮之弊二者一曰游民二曰異端游民衆
則力本者少異端盛則務農者稀夫民所以樂
於游墮者何也盖起於不均不平之横征病於
豪強之兼併小民無所利於農也以為逐藝而
===
食猶可以為苟且求生之計且夫均天下之田
然後可以責天下之耕今夫里閈之小民剥於
汚吏豪強者深矣散食於四方者衆矣大率計
今天下之民其有田者一二而無田者常八九
也以八九不耕之民坐食一二之粟其勢不得
不困然而散一二有田者之業以為八九自耕
之養其勢未嘗不足議者病游民之衆也或有
逐商之說然臣以為游民之固本於不得已也
而又無所變置而徒為之逐臣懼夫商之不安
於商也臣竊謂今日之弊源已深更化者當端

punctuated:
為之計矣。此則制國無紀，潰亂不時，盖昏亂衰世之政馬。盖臣前所謂起於游墮、病於冗雜之弊，亦畧有同於是。陛下今所方欲改轍而易海內之觀者，臣謂今日游墮之弊有二，冗雜之弊有三。此天下之所以長坐於困乏，而志士至今憤惋而嘆息者也。
其所謂游墮之弊二者，一曰游民，二曰異端。游民衆，則力本者少；異端盛，則務農者稀。夫民所以樂於游墮者，何也？盖起於不均不平之横征，病於豪強之兼併，小民無所利於農也，以為逐藝而食，猶可以為苟且求生之計。且夫均天下之田，然後可以責天下之耕。今夫里閈之小民，剥於汚吏豪強者深矣，散食於四方者衆矣。大率計今天下之民，其有田者一二，而無田者常八九也。以八九不耕之民，坐食一二之粟，其勢不得不困。然而散一二有田者之業，以為八九自耕之養，其勢未嘗不足。議者病游民之衆也，或有逐商之說。然臣以為游民之固本於不得已也，而又無所變置，而徒為之逐，臣懼夫商之不安於商也。臣竊謂今日之弊，源已深，更化者當端
translation_en:
…devise a plan to deal with it. This is governing a state without orderly principles, with collapse and disorder liable to arise at any time: surely the government of a benighted and declining age [?]. The abuses your servant mentioned earlier—arising from idleness and aggravated by excessive numbers and complexity—are also somewhat similar to these. Your Majesty now wishes to change course and transform the condition of the realm. Your servant holds that today there are two abuses associated with idleness and three associated with excessive numbers and complexity. These are why the realm remains trapped in want, and why men of aspiration still lament and sigh in indignation.
Of the two abuses associated with idleness, the first is an unattached populace, and the second is heterodox teachings. When unattached people are numerous, few devote their strength to the fundamental occupation of agriculture; when heterodox teachings flourish, few attend to farming. Why do people take pleasure in idleness? It originates in arbitrary exactions imposed unevenly and unfairly, and is aggravated by the engrossment of land by the powerful. Ordinary people find no advantage in farming and believe that making a living by pursuing a craft at least offers an expedient means of survival. Moreover, only after distributing the land of the realm equitably can one require the people of the realm to cultivate it. Today, ordinary villagers suffer grievously from exploitation by corrupt officials and powerful families, and many scatter in every direction to seek a livelihood. Roughly reckoning the people of the realm today, only one or two in ten own land, while fully eight or nine in ten have none. With eight or nine who do not cultivate consuming the grain of the one or two, hardship is inevitable. Yet if the holdings of the one or two landowners were distributed to provide the eight or nine with sustenance through their own cultivation, there need be no insufficiency. Those discussing the matter deplore the multitude of unattached people, and some propose expelling merchants. Your servant, however, believes that people become unattached fundamentally because they have no alternative. If no arrangements are changed and they are merely expelled, your servant fears that merchants will be unable to pursue their trade in peace. Your servant humbly considers that the abuses of the present day are already deeply rooted, and that those undertaking reform should begin by setting in order…

text:
其緒而緩理之理而無緒勢将驅力農之民而
商而又将驅力商之民而盜也天下為盜國不
可久其便莫若頒限田之法嚴兼併之禁而又
擇循良仁愛惻怛之吏以撫勞之法以定其世
業禁以防其姦貪吏以時其安緝游民其将歸
乎若夫異端者盖本無超俗利世之智而徒竊
其減額逃刑之利不工不商不農不士以自便
其身且其倡無父無君之教於天下将使流風
之未可已焉此其為害甚明故臣不待深辯然
臣竊悼俗之方弊也禿首黄冠充斥道路珠宫
===
瓊宇照耀雲漢此風未艾效慕者眾非所以令
眾庶見也非所以端風正紀之要體也故臣願
陛下嚴異端之禁斥道佛之說敕令此輩悉歸之農
其有不如令者許有司罪治不赦盖非惟崇力
本之風抑且彰教化之道此臣拳拳所望於
陛下之至意也其所謂冗雜之弊三者一曰冗員二
曰冗兵三曰冗費冗員之弊必澄冗兵之弊必
汰冗費之弊必省三冗去而財裕矣夫聖人所
以制祿以養天下之吏與兵者何也吏有治人
之明則食之也兵有敵人之勇則食之也是其

…the threads of the problem, and unravel them gradually. To attempt to put matters in order without finding those threads will inevitably drive people who work diligently at farming into commerce, and then drive those who work diligently at commerce into banditry. If all under Heaven become bandits, the state cannot endure. The most effective course would be to promulgate a law limiting landholdings, strictly enforce the prohibition on engrossing land, and select upright, benevolent, compassionate officials to care for and comfort the people. Let the law secure their hereditary livelihoods, prohibitions restrain their dishonesty and greed, and officials attend in timely fashion to their peace and settled condition [?]. Would not the unsettled populace then return?
As for the followers of heterodox teachings, they possess no wisdom that transcends the ordinary or benefits the world; they merely appropriate the advantages of reductions in assessed obligations [?] and evasion of punishment. They act as neither artisans, merchants, farmers, nor scholars, seeking only their own ease. Moreover, they propagate throughout the realm teachings that acknowledge neither father nor sovereign, thereby allowing their lingering influence to spread without end. The harm they cause is plain, so your servant need not argue it at length. Yet your servant privately grieves at the present deterioration of customs: shaven-headed monks and yellow-capped Daoists crowd the roads, while pearl palaces and jade halls shine up to the Milky Way. This fashion has not abated, and many admire and imitate it. This is no example to set before the common people, nor does it accord with the essential principles of rectifying customs and restoring proper order. Your servant therefore wishes Your Majesty to enforce strict prohibitions against heterodoxy, reject Daoist and Buddhist doctrines, and issue an edict ordering all these people to return to farming. For any who disobey the order, authorize the responsible officials to punish them without pardon. This would not only encourage devotion to agriculture, the fundamental occupation, but also make manifest the way of moral instruction. Such is the heartfelt wish that your servant most earnestly places in Your Majesty.
The abuses of superfluity and excess mentioned above are three: first, superfluous personnel; second, superfluous soldiers; and third, superfluous expenditure. The abuse of superfluous personnel must be cleared away, that of superfluous soldiers eliminated, and that of superfluous expenditure curtailed. …they are maintained because they possess discernment and courage. If any lack discernment or courage, they should not eat unless they till the soil, nor be clothed unless they raise silkworms. Why? The former kings, too, were sparing in granting stipends to those who performed no service. What, then, is the present condition of the officials and soldiers throughout the realm? Your servant does not wish to deprive all the realm’s officials and soldiers of their stipends. I merely observe that among those serving in prefectures and counties, some are feeble and incapable of discharging their duties, yet draw stipends while doing nothing; among those enrolled on the military registers, some are old, weak, and unfit for service, yet receive provisions without justification. Moreover, there are too many avenues to office through monetary contributions, and too many officials appointed through hereditary privilege. Responsibility for inspection and scrutiny is not rigorously enforced, and methods of training and selection are deficient. Your servant therefore wishes to subject all these men to scrutiny and dismissal where appropriate. This would do much to eliminate superfluous personnel and improper claims, and to ease the people’s burdens [?].
As for the abuses of excessive expenditure, I cannot enumerate them all. To discuss only the largest and most conspicuous: banquets and grants in the rear palace must be restrained; support for heterodox teachings must not be excessive; and construction projects must be curtailed. Your Majesty rectifies your own conduct to lead others, exercises self-restraint, and lives frugally. In these three matters, there is certainly no ground for criticism of you. Yet I humbly observe that, from the vast realm with its multitude of people and resources, tribute from the Nine Provinces and the Four Seas, levies of every foot of silk and grain of rice, and taxes on mountains, forests, rivers, and marshes converge day and night upon the Grand Granary. These receipts may well be called abundant. Nevertheless, the state’s finances remain far from ample, and its resources far from sufficient. I believe there must be something draining them [?]. Furthermore, when those above levy one unit upon those below, the latter regularly expend ten to supply it. Because of losses along the roads and the costs of transport by water and land, one unit of money in the capital costs the countryside a hundred; a hundred in the palace treasury costs the people’s households ten thousand. How boundless is the expenditure of the resources of a million households upon a single banquet, a single grant, or a single object supplied for amusement! …even today, there are expenditures that have not been fully curtailed. Your servant has heard that, if all the revenues of the realm are used to provide for its people, there can be no insufficiency. But when resources are squandered on unnecessary expenses, this inevitably leads to arbitrary levies and excessive exactions, which will not cease until the whole realm suffers hunger and cold, starvation and freezing, utter ruin and exhaustion. Reading the Records of the Grand Historian, your servant saw that when King Wen of Zhou received the Mandate, his territory measured no more than one hundred li square. Yet rulers from every quarter came in succession to his state, and the ceremonies for feasting, rewarding, and welcoming them could hardly have been dispensed with altogether. Nevertheless, the common people then each had enough and did not suffer from hunger or cold. Thus the people recited a poem saying: “Diligently our king labors, ordering the four quarters.” They were celebrating him. When rule passed to his descendants, the revenues of eight hundred states supported a single man. Surely he should have enjoyed great abundance and freedom from anxiety; yet the people instead became displaced and impoverished, until verses about yellow birds and separation were composed.
From this your servant sees that when a ruler restrains his own consumption to benefit others, success is readily achieved; when he expands expenditure and exacts heavy levies, his task becomes difficult. This is why your servant so earnestly urges Your Majesty to reduce unnecessary expenditure.
In your policy question, Your Majesty said to your servant: “It is fundamentally [?] brought about by my own unworthiness and limited understanding: above, I cannot assist in harmonizing the workings of cosmic transformation; below, I cannot invigorate good government. I am truly troubled and ashamed.” These are words of Your Majesty’s anxious diligence, words of self-reproach like those of Yu and Tang. Yet your servant believes that Your Majesty must do more than merely utter these words: you must strive to put them into practice. A ruler’s words differ from those of scholars and commoners. If even once they fail to be borne out, the realm will treat them lightly. Thereafter, even when he has good intentions and sound policies, people will be alarmed and doubtful, and will not believe him. translation_en:
…empty words from Your Majesty. Why? They have indeed seen such pronouncements, but have yet to see their benefits. Now Your Majesty again puts such a policy question to your servant. I believe that what is needed is simply to give practical effect to your concern and diligence. To do so, you must swiftly put your servant’s proposals into practice. Yet everything I have presented above responds point by point to matters raised in the imperial policy question. In sum, the means of remedying abuses and benefiting the world have not yet been fully set forth here. Allow your servant to complete his account.
When the resources of mountains and marshes have not been fully developed for cultivation, the realm will certainly suffer from a shortage of farmland. Now the lands east of the capital, in the regions of Cai, Deng, Qi, and Lu, were anciently renowned as wealthy, populous, and powerful states. Much of the revenue of the Three Dynasties came from here. Since the Han and Tang, traces of the ditches, channels, embankments, and waterways [?] through which eminent ministers and worthy prefects improved agriculture and supplemented state resources have often survived. Yet today these lands have all become empty wastes of thatch grass and reeds. This is what the ancients meant by the productive capacity of the land remaining untapped. Those whom Your Majesty appoints to govern this territory merely discharge their duties perfunctorily, and none can shoulder responsibility for this concern. Thus northerners continually sit dependent on supplies from the southeast. When even a minor crop failure or famine interrupts those supplies, they tumble into ditches, unable to sustain themselves: the land’s productive capacity has not been fully developed.
Your servant believes that Your Majesty’s best course would be to hold prefects and county magistrates to stricter standards, taking great care to select men of energy and ability who loyally serve the state. Appoint them to govern these lands and have them devote themselves exclusively to agricultural improvement. Let the court relax its prohibitions and restrictions and allow them discretion to act as circumstances require, assessing their agricultural achievements solely on this basis. Then men like Zhao Guo will surely emerge within the realm. Before several decades have passed, the lands north of the Yangzi…

title: 嘉靖十一年進士登科錄
text:
之田應與江南類可省江淮數百萬之財賦而
紓北人饑寒凍餒之急一舉而利二焉大惠也
陛下能斷而行之大勇也或曰非不欲行也如東南
異宜何臣請有以折之夫今日所謂空虚荒瘠
無用之地者非向時所謂富實而所托賴以興
起之本區乎昔以富實今以荒虚臣誠未喻其
說亦曰存夫人爾魏人許下之屯可見矣方棗
祗為屯許之畫也當時亦誠見其落落難合洎
其成也操終賴之省粟數萬今天下之大又安
知其無能為棗祗者乎臣是以願
===
陛下以此為田利課則山澤墾矣臣又聞之山澤不
征市梁無禁王者所以通天下大公大同之制
也自漢桑弘羊以剥刻之術媚上而征榷之法
始詳歷代因之而不革大公之制未聞也然臣
終以此為後世衰亂苟且之政今
朝廷之取民茶有征酒有榷山澤有租魚鹽有課
自一草木以上之利莫不悉籠而歸之公其取
下悉矣夫上取下悉則其勢窮夫獸窮則逐人
窮則詐今
陛下之民將詐矣司國議者非不知其勢之不可以

punctuated:
之田應與江南類，可省江淮數百萬之財賦，而紓北人饑寒凍餒之急，一舉而利二焉，大惠也。陛下能斷而行之，大勇也。或曰：「非不欲行也，如東南異宜何？」臣請有以折之。夫今日所謂空虚荒瘠無用之地者，非向時所謂富實而所托賴以興起之本區乎？昔以富實，今以荒虚，臣誠未喻其說。亦曰存夫人爾。魏人許下之屯可見矣。方棗祗為屯許之畫也，當時亦誠見其落落難合；洎其成也，操終賴之省粟數萬。今天下之大，又安知其無能為棗祗者乎？臣是以願陛下以此為田利課，則山澤墾矣。

臣又聞之，山澤不征，市梁無禁，王者所以通天下大公大同之制也。自漢桑弘羊以剥刻之術媚上，而征榷之法始詳，歷代因之而不革，大公之制未聞也。然臣終以此為後世衰亂苟且之政。今朝廷之取民，茶有征，酒有榷，山澤有租，魚鹽有課，自一草木以上之利，莫不悉籠而歸之公，其取下悉矣。夫上取下悉，則其勢窮。夫獸窮則逐，人窮則詐。今陛下之民將詐矣。司國議者非不知其勢之不可以
translation_en:
…the fields should become like those south of the Yangzi. This could save several million in tax revenues drawn from the Jiang-Huai region and relieve the urgent distress of northerners suffering from hunger and cold. To secure two benefits with a single measure would be a great act of benevolence. For Your Majesty to resolve upon it and carry it out would be an act of great courage. Some may say, “It is not that we do not wish to implement it, but what of the different conditions in the southeast?” Your servant asks leave to refute this. Are the lands now called empty, barren, and useless not the very heartland once called wealthy and well supplied, upon which the rise of ruling powers depended? Once prosperous, now desolate: your servant truly cannot understand this argument. It depends only upon having the right men. The agricultural colonies established by the men of Wei at Xu demonstrate this. When Zao Zhi devised his plan for agricultural colonies at Xu, it indeed seemed at the time far removed from practical circumstances and difficult to realize. Once it succeeded, however, Cao Cao ultimately relied upon it to save tens of thousands of measures of grain. In all the vastness of the realm today, how can we know that there is no one capable of doing what Zao Zhi did? Your servant therefore wishes Your Majesty to make this the criterion for assessing agricultural development; then the hills and marshlands will be brought under cultivation.

Your servant has also heard that levying no taxes on hills and marshlands and imposing no restrictions on markets and fishing weirs were the means by which true kings extended throughout the realm a system of universal equity and common benefit. Beginning with Sang Hongyang of the Han, who flattered his sovereign through methods of harsh exaction, the laws governing taxation and monopolies became elaborate. Successive dynasties followed them without reform, and a system of universal equity has not been heard of. Yet your servant regards these, after all, as expedient policies of later ages of decline and disorder. Today, in the court’s exactions from the people, tea is taxed, wine is subject to monopoly, hills and marshlands yield rents, and fish and salt bear levies. Every source of profit, down to a single plant or tree, is comprehensively gathered into government hands. Its exactions from those below are exhaustive. When those above take everything from those below, the latter are driven to extremity. Beasts driven to extremity give chase [?]; people driven to extremity resort to deception. Now Your Majesty’s people are about to resort to deception. Those responsible for deliberating on affairs of state are not unaware that this situation cannot…

title: 嘉靖十一年進士登科錄
text:
久也然而明知其弊而冒之者誠曰國家利權
之所在也臣以為利不勝義義苟未安利之何
益况又有不利者在乎臣聞之王者所以總制
六合而鎮服民心張大國體者固在道德之厚
薄不問財賦之有無臣觀征利之說不出於豐
大之國恒出於衰亂之世纖纖然與民爭利者
匹夫之事也萬乘而下行匹夫之事則其國辱
非豐大之時所尚也
陛下何不曠然為人所難思大公之法去衰亂之政
今天下人士爭言曰惜哉漢唐宋不能舍匹夫
之利以利人至我
明天子然後能以天子之大體鎮服民心焉
陛下何久於此焉不為也臣願
陛下息山林關市之征焉使大聖人所作為過於人
萬萬也若夫悉推富民之術則平糴之法不可
不立也常平之倉不可不設也奢侈之禁不可
不嚴也凡若此者史策之載可考
陛下果能舉而行之成典具在故臣不必深論之也
由臣前所陳而言之均田也擇吏也去冗也省
費也由臣後所陳而言之闢土也薄征也通利

punctuated:
久也。然而明知其弊而冒之者，誠曰國家利權之所在也。臣以為利不勝義，義苟未安，利之何益？况又有不利者在乎？臣聞之，王者所以總制六合而鎮服民心、張大國體者，固在道德之厚薄，不問財賦之有無。臣觀征利之說，不出於豐大之國，恒出於衰亂之世。纖纖然與民爭利者，匹夫之事也。萬乘而下行匹夫之事，則其國辱，非豐大之時所尚也。陛下何不曠然為人所難，思大公之法，去衰亂之政？今天下人士爭言曰：「惜哉！漢唐宋不能舍匹夫之利以利人，至我明天子，然後能以天子之大體鎮服民心焉。」陛下何久於此焉不為也？臣願陛下息山林關市之征焉，使大聖人所作為過於人萬萬也。若夫悉推富民之術，則平糴之法不可不立也，常平之倉不可不設也，奢侈之禁不可不嚴也。凡若此者，史策之載可考。陛下果能舉而行之，成典具在，故臣不必深論之也。
由臣前所陳而言之，均田也，擇吏也，去冗也，省費也；由臣後所陳而言之，闢土也，薄征也，通利
translation_en:
…endure. Yet those who clearly recognize its evils and nevertheless persist in it truly say that this is where the state's control over sources of profit lies. Your servant believes that profit cannot outweigh righteousness. If a measure is not justified by righteousness, what benefit can its profits bring? Moreover, does it not also entail disadvantages? Your servant has heard that a true king's ability to govern all within the six directions, command the allegiance of the people's hearts, and enhance the dignity of the state rests on the depth of his virtue, not on the presence or absence of fiscal revenues. Your servant observes that proposals to exact profits do not arise in flourishing and powerful states, but invariably emerge in ages of decline and disorder. Pettily competing with the people for profit is the business of a common man. If the ruler of ten thousand chariots stoops to acting as a common man, his state is dishonored. This is not what is esteemed in times of prosperity and greatness.
Why does Your Majesty not act with magnanimity to accomplish what others find difficult, consider measures of impartial public benefit, and abolish the policies of declining and disordered ages? Now gentlemen throughout the realm vie in saying: “What a pity that the Han, Tang, and Song could not relinquish the profits of a common man to benefit the people! Only with our Ming Son of Heaven has a ruler been able to command the allegiance of the people's hearts through the broad principles befitting the Son of Heaven.” Why has Your Majesty so long failed to act on this matter? Your servant wishes that Your Majesty would end the levies on mountains and forests, customs barriers and markets, so that the deeds of a great sage might surpass those of others ten thousand times over. As for fully implementing the means of enriching the people, a system of grain purchases to stabilize prices must be established, Ever-Normal Granaries must be instituted, and prohibitions on extravagance must be strictly enforced. All such measures can be examined in the historical records. If Your Majesty can indeed put them into practice, established precedents are all available; your servant therefore need not discuss them at length.
To summarize what your servant presented earlier: equalize landholdings, select officials carefully, eliminate superfluous personnel, and reduce expenditure. To summarize what your servant presented later: open land to cultivation, reduce levies, facilitate the circulation of wealth…

title: 嘉靖十一年進士登科錄
text:
也禁奢也田均而業厚吏良而俗阜冗去而蠹
除費省而用裕土闢而利廣征薄而息寛利通
而財流奢禁而富益八政立而王制備矣
陛下果能行臣之言又何憂於百姓之凍餒饑寒流
離又何至於有盜賊之警又何患夫不順夫道
而歸乎化哉通變宜時之道其或悉備於此然
臣以為此數者皆不足為
陛下之難所患人主一心不能清虛寡欲以為寛民
養物之要則雖有善政美令未暇及行盖崇高
富貴之地固易為驕奢淫逸之所是故明主重
===
內治也故古之賢王遐觀遠慮居尊而慮其危
處富而懼其溢履滿而防其傾誠以定志慮而
節逸欲固寅畏而禁微邪也故堯曰兢舜曰業
禹曰孜湯曰檢臣以為數聖人固得治心之要
矣臣嘗讀漢書見漢武帝之為君方其臨軒策
士奮志六經也雖三代之英主不能過焉洎其
中年多欲一念不能自勝公孫弘桑弘羊張騫
卜式文成五利之輩各乘其隙而售之卒使更
變紛然天下坐是大耗臣是以知人主一心不
可使有所嗜好形見於外少有沉溺為禍必大

punctuated:
也，禁奢也。田均而業厚，吏良而俗阜，冗去而蠹除，費省而用裕，土闢而利廣，征薄而息寛，利通而財流，奢禁而富益。八政立而王制備矣。陛下果能行臣之言，又何憂於百姓之凍餒饑寒流離？又何至於有盜賊之警？又何患夫不順夫道而歸乎化哉？通變宜時之道，其或悉備於此。然臣以為，此數者皆不足為陛下之難。所患人主一心不能清虛寡欲，以為寛民養物之要，則雖有善政美令，未暇及行。盖崇高富貴之地，固易為驕奢淫逸之所，是故明主重內治也。
故古之賢王，遐觀遠慮，居尊而慮其危，處富而懼其溢，履滿而防其傾，誠以定志慮而節逸欲，固寅畏而禁微邪也。故堯曰兢，舜曰業，禹曰孜，湯曰檢。臣以為數聖人固得治心之要矣。臣嘗讀《漢書》，見漢武帝之為君，方其臨軒策士，奮志六經也，雖三代之英主不能過焉。洎其中年，多欲一念不能自勝，公孫弘、桑弘羊、張騫、卜式、文成、五利之輩，各乘其隙而售之，卒使更變紛然，天下坐是大耗。臣是以知人主一心，不可使有所嗜好形見於外，少有沉溺，為禍必大。
translation_en:
…and prohibiting extravagance. When land is equitably distributed, livelihoods become substantial; when officials are good, the people prosper; when superfluous personnel are removed, those who prey upon the people are eliminated; when expenditure is reduced, resources suffice; when land is opened up, benefits expand; when levies are light, the people have greater respite; when channels of profit are unobstructed, wealth circulates; and when extravagance is prohibited, prosperity increases. Once these eight measures of government are established, the institutions of true kingship will be complete. If Your Majesty can indeed act upon your servant’s words, why need you worry about the common people freezing, starving, suffering hunger and cold, or wandering displaced? How could alarms about bandits arise? Why need you fear that the people would fail to follow the Way and submit to your transforming influence? The methods of adapting to change and meeting the needs of the times may perhaps all be contained here. Yet your servant believes that none of these measures should present a difficulty for Your Majesty. What is to be feared is that the ruler’s mind cannot remain clear, unburdened, and free of excessive desires—the essential basis for easing the people’s burdens and nurturing all things. In that case, even good policies and excellent commands will go unimplemented. For a position of eminence, wealth, and honor readily becomes a setting for arrogance, extravagance, excess, and indolence. Thus an enlightened ruler attaches importance to governing himself within.
Therefore, the worthy kings of antiquity looked far ahead and considered distant consequences. In exalted positions they pondered the dangers; amid wealth they feared excess; at the height of abundance they guarded against downfall. Through sincerity they steadied their purposes and thoughts and restrained desires for ease; they maintained reverent apprehension and checked the slightest stirrings of waywardness. Thus Yao spoke of vigilance, Shun of caution, Yu of diligence, and Tang of restraint. Your servant believes that these sages indeed grasped the essentials of governing the mind. Your servant once read the History of the Han and observed Emperor Wu of Han’s conduct as ruler. When he personally presided over the policy examination of scholars and devoted his aspirations to the Six Classics, even the illustrious rulers of the Three Dynasties could not surpass him. By his middle years, however, he had become full of desires and could not master even a single thought. Gongsun Hong, Sang Hongyang, Zhang Qian, Bu Shi, and such men as Wencheng and Wuli each exploited an opening to press their own proposals upon him. In the end, they brought about a welter of changes, and the realm was gravely depleted as a result. From this your servant understands that a ruler must not allow the preferences of his mind to show outwardly. Even a little indulgence will inevitably bring great calamity.

title: 嘉靖十一年進士登科錄
text:
故願
陛下靜虛恬慮以為清心節欲之本毋以深居無事
而好逸遊毋以海宇平清而事逺夷毋以物力
豐實而興土木毋以聰明英斷而尚刑名毋以
財賦富盛而事奢侈毋羨邪說而惑神仙澄心
正極省慮虛涵心澄則日明慮省則日精精明
之運旁燭無疆舉天下功業惟吾所建者豈止
於富民生足衣食而已哉臣始以治弊治法為
陛下告終以清心寡欲為
陛下勉蓋非有驚世絕俗之論以警動
===
陛下然直意以為
陛下之所以策臣者蓋欲聞剴切時病之說故畧敢
盡其私憂過計之辭衷情所激誠不知其言之
猶有所憚亦不知其言之猶有隱惟
陛下寬其狂易諒其朴直而一賜覽之天下幸甚臣
謹對

punctuated: 故願陛下靜虛恬慮，以為清心節欲之本。毋以深居無事而好逸遊，毋以海宇平清而事逺夷，毋以物力豐實而興土木，毋以聰明英斷而尚刑名，毋以財賦富盛而事奢侈，毋羨邪說而惑神仙。澄心正極，省慮虛涵。心澄則日明，慮省則日精。精明之運，旁燭無疆，舉天下功業，惟吾所建者，豈止於富民生、足衣食而已哉？臣始以治弊治法為陛下告，終以清心寡欲為陛下勉，蓋非有驚世絕俗之論以警動陛下。然直意以為，陛下之所以策臣者，蓋欲聞剴切時病之說，故畧敢盡其私憂過計之辭。衷情所激，誠不知其言之猶有所憚，亦不知其言之猶有隱。惟陛下寬其狂易，諒其朴直，而一賜覽之，天下幸甚。臣謹對。
translation_en:
Therefore I hope that Your Majesty will remain still and receptive, keeping your thoughts tranquil, as the foundation for purifying the mind and restraining desires. Do not let secluded residence and freedom from affairs lead to a fondness for idle excursions; do not let peace throughout the realm lead to undertakings among distant foreign peoples; do not let abundant material resources lead to building projects; do not let intelligence and decisive judgment lead to an excessive regard for penal and administrative techniques; do not let ample revenues lead to extravagance; and do not admire heterodox teachings and become deluded by the immortals. Clarify your mind and set upright the supreme standard; reduce distracting thoughts and cultivate an open, receptive mind. As the mind grows clear, it becomes daily more discerning; as distracting thoughts diminish, it becomes daily more refined. The workings of this refined discernment will illuminate everything without limit. With all the achievements of the realm yours to establish, how could the result be confined merely to enriching the people's livelihood and providing sufficient clothing and food?

Your servant began by addressing Your Majesty on remedying abuses and methods of governance, and concludes by urging Your Majesty to purify the mind and lessen desires. I have no startling or extraordinary argument with which to rouse Your Majesty. Yet I sincerely believe that Your Majesty put this policy question to me because you wished to hear arguments bearing directly upon the maladies of our time. Thus I have ventured to give some full expression to my private anxieties and perhaps excessive apprehensions. Moved by my innermost feelings, I truly know of nothing that I have still feared to say, nor of anything that my words have still concealed. I ask only that Your Majesty pardon my rashness, understand my plain sincerity, and graciously read this response. It would be a great blessing for all under Heaven. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

title: 嘉靖十一年進士登科錄
text:
臣孔天胤
臣對臣聞帝王之治敦本以厚天下之生達權
以通天下之變則天德孚而王道成矣夫民生
也者邦家所恃以為基者也然而厚生之道有
本存焉事變也者治忽所乘以為幾者也然而
通變之道有權存焉夫其本之在是也而弗敦
之以厚天下之生則化必不溥澤必不深而邦
家之基或將匪安夫其權之在是也而弗達之
以通天下之變則弊弗可釐滯弗可起而治忽
之幾將有大可畏者矣是以聖帝明王之治天
===
下也代天理物必以厚生為先更化善治必以
通變為先惟厚生也則必自其本之所在者而
敦之躬行於上而作則於下焉經理之密而講
畫之詳焉必期化溥澤深而後已惟通變也則
必自其權之所在者而達之察時審勢而化裁
之焉隨幾應用而神明之焉必期弊釐滯起而
後已化溥澤深則群生和萬物育而邦基日以
益固弊釐滯起則德富有業日新而治幾日以
益熈由是天德孚於上下王道成於始終而有
以昭帝王之盛者固如是矣恭惟

punctuated:
臣孔天胤。

臣對：臣聞帝王之治，敦本以厚天下之生，達權以通天下之變，則天德孚而王道成矣。夫民生也者，邦家所恃以為基者也；然而厚生之道，有本存焉。事變也者，治忽所乘以為幾者也；然而通變之道，有權存焉。夫其本之在是也，而弗敦之以厚天下之生，則化必不溥，澤必不深，而邦家之基或將匪安。夫其權之在是也，而弗達之以通天下之變，則弊弗可釐，滯弗可起，而治忽之幾將有大可畏者矣。是以聖帝明王之治天下也，代天理物，必以厚生為先；更化善治，必以通變為先。惟厚生也，則必自其本之所在者而敦之，躬行於上而作則於下焉，經理之密而講畫之詳焉，必期化溥澤深而後已。惟通變也，則必自其權之所在者而達之，察時審勢而化裁之焉，隨幾應用而神明之焉，必期弊釐滯起而後已。化溥澤深，則群生和，萬物育，而邦基日以益固；弊釐滯起，則德富有，業日新，而治幾日以益熈。由是天德孚於上下，王道成於始終，而有以昭帝王之盛者，固如是矣。恭惟
translation_en:
Your servant, Kong Tianyin.

Your servant replies: I have heard that, in the government of emperors and kings, strengthening the foundations enriches the livelihood of all under Heaven, while understanding discretionary judgment enables them to respond to changing circumstances throughout the realm. Then Heaven’s virtue wins trust, and the Kingly Way is realized. The people’s livelihood is the foundation upon which the state relies; yet the way to enrich livelihood has its roots. Changing circumstances are the pivotal occasions upon which order or disorder turns; yet the way to respond to change requires discretionary judgment. If these roots are present but are not strengthened to enrich the livelihood of all under Heaven, transforming influence will surely fail to spread widely, beneficence will surely fail to penetrate deeply, and the foundations of the state may become insecure. If such discretionary judgment is called for but is not understood and exercised to respond to changes throughout the realm, abuses cannot be corrected and stagnation cannot be overcome. The turning points between order and disorder will then hold much to fear.

Thus, when sage emperors and enlightened kings governed all under Heaven, they gave priority to enriching livelihood as they ordered things on Heaven’s behalf, and to responding to change as they reformed administration and improved government. To enrich livelihood, they necessarily strengthened its very roots: they personally practiced what was right above and established a model for those below, managed affairs meticulously, and deliberated and planned in detail. They did not rest until their transforming influence spread widely and their beneficence penetrated deeply. To respond to change, they necessarily understood and exercised the discretionary judgment it required: they examined the times and assessed circumstances, adapting and deciding accordingly; they responded to each incipient development and applied their judgment with inspired discernment. They did not rest until abuses were corrected and stagnation overcome.

When transforming influence spreads widely and beneficence penetrates deeply, all living beings are in harmony, the myriad things flourish, and the foundations of the state grow firmer each day. When abuses are corrected and stagnation overcome, virtue becomes abundant, achievement is renewed daily, and the workings of government grow ever more flourishing. Through this, Heaven’s virtue wins trust among those above and below, and the Kingly Way is realized from beginning to end. Such, indeed, is how the splendor of emperors and kings is made manifest. I reverently consider…

title: 嘉靖十一年進士登科錄
text:
皇帝陛下膺
天眷命纘承
大統臨御以來視民如傷望道未見乃進臣等於
廷策以天下之務臣莊誦竊嘆以為
聖人建其有極敷錫厥福端崇理本明燭化機固
有神明之道而乃以詢之末學之臣臣愚何足
以知之然對揚
休命不敢以終黙焉臣甞讀周之書有曰惟天地
萬物父母惟元后作民父母言天生民而立之
君使司牧之也讀易之辭有曰后以財成天地
===
之道輔相天地之宜言明王代天理物奉若天
道也是知奉若天道莫大乎子民子民之道莫
大乎厚生厚生之道莫大乎遂其所安所欲之
情遂其所安所欲之情則又莫大乎重農桑之
務足衣食之源衣食足則民情遂民情遂則民
生厚民生厚則教化行風俗美陰陽調風雨時
群生和庶類殖民沴物眚之異寇賊姦宄之變
莫不盡銷諸福之物可致之祥莫不畢至而王
道有終矣是以古昔先王繼天立極開物成務
必以此先焉粤稽庖羲氏之王天下也首教民

道有終矣是以古昔先王繼天立極開物成務
必以此先焉粤稽庖羲氏之王天下也首教民
punctuated:
皇帝陛下膺天眷命，纘承大統。臨御以來，視民如傷，望道未見，乃進臣等於廷，策以天下之務。臣莊誦竊嘆，以為聖人建其有極，敷錫厥福，端崇理本，明燭化機，固有神明之道，而乃以詢之末學之臣，臣愚何足以知之？然對揚休命，不敢以終黙焉。
臣甞讀周之書，有曰：「惟天地，萬物父母；惟元后，作民父母。」言天生民而立之君，使司牧之也。讀易之辭，有曰：「后以財成天地之道，輔相天地之宜。」言明王代天理物，奉若天道也。是知奉若天道，莫大乎子民；子民之道，莫大乎厚生；厚生之道，莫大乎遂其所安所欲之情；遂其所安所欲之情，則又莫大乎重農桑之務，足衣食之源。衣食足則民情遂，民情遂則民生厚，民生厚則教化行、風俗美、陰陽調、風雨時、群生和、庶類殖，民沴物眚之異、寇賊姦宄之變，莫不盡銷；諸福之物、可致之祥，莫不畢至，而王道有終矣。
是以古昔先王繼天立極，開物成務，必以此先焉。粤稽庖羲氏之王天下也，首教民
translation_en:
… Your Majesty the Emperor has received Heaven’s gracious mandate and succeeded to the great imperial succession. Since taking the throne, you have cared for the people as though they were injured and sought the Way as though you had not yet seen it. You have now summoned us, your servants, to court and posed policy questions concerning the affairs of the realm. Solemnly reading them, I marvel to myself: the sage establishes the supreme standard and bestows blessings upon all; he upholds the root of good order and clearly illuminates the workings of transformation. Surely he possesses a divinely discerning Way, yet he asks about these matters of a servant of such meager learning. How could I, in my ignorance, know enough to answer? Nevertheless, in responding to and extolling your gracious command, I dare not remain silent throughout.
I once read in the Documents of Zhou: “Heaven and Earth are the parents of all things; the sovereign acts as the parent of the people.” This means that Heaven gives birth to the people and establishes a ruler over them to oversee and shepherd them. I read in the words of the Book of Changes: “The ruler regulates and brings to completion the Way of Heaven and Earth, and assists what is fitting in Heaven and Earth.” This means that an enlightened king orders all things on Heaven’s behalf and reverently accords with Heaven’s Way. From this we know that nothing is more important in following Heaven’s Way than caring for the people as one’s children; nothing is more important in caring for them than enriching their livelihoods; and nothing is more important in enriching their livelihoods than satisfying their desires for security and the things they seek. To satisfy these desires, nothing is more important than giving weight to agriculture and sericulture and ensuring ample sources of clothing and food. When clothing and food are sufficient, the people’s desires are satisfied; when their desires are satisfied, their livelihoods flourish. When their livelihoods flourish, moral instruction takes effect, customs improve, yin and yang are balanced, wind and rain arrive in season, living beings exist in harmony, and all kinds of creatures multiply. Anomalies that bring affliction to the people and harm to other things, and disturbances caused by bandits, robbers, and evildoers within and without, will all disappear. Every manifestation of blessing and every auspicious sign that can be brought forth will arrive, and the kingly Way will reach its fulfillment.
Thus, when the former kings of antiquity succeeded Heaven in establishing the supreme standard, opened up the potential of things, and brought affairs to completion, they invariably gave these matters priority. Looking back to when Paoxi ruled all under Heaven, he first taught the people …

title: 嘉靖十一年進士登科錄
text:
耒耜而耕之制以興耕之制興而食之源以開
矣軒轅氏之王天下也首教民衣服而蠶之制
以興蠶之制興而衣之源以開矣堯命羲和授
民時舜命益稷興民利禹湯平成允殖文武咸
和永清率是道也然三代之道固無不同而成
周之法尤為至備于是天子有籍田之典焉一
撥三推庶民助以終畝也王后有親蠶之典焉
繰三盆手世婦布於蠶宮也夫君后至貴也而
以服田野之勞誠念夫稼穡之艱難小民之所
依王業之根本在是也故服勞以為天下先焉
===
是以當時之人男則服事乎耕焉所謂亦服爾
耕十千維耦也女則服事乎蠶焉所謂女執懿
筐爰求柔桑也夫天下至大也而皆力農桑之
務誠念夫食之資於耕衣之資於蠶而所安所
欲之樂在是也故協極以光其本焉今觀無逸
之書七月之詩帝王所傳心法之要可繹思矣
成王以之致四十年之平周家以之永八百年
之祚良以敦天下之本而厚天下之生如是也
聖制曰民之所安所欲者必首之以衣與食使無衣
無食未免有凍餓死亡流離困苦之害夫匪耕則

是以當時之人，男則服事乎耕焉，所謂「亦服爾耕，十千維耦」也；女則服事乎蠶焉，所謂「女執懿筐，爰求柔桑」也。夫天下至大也，而皆力農桑之務，誠念夫食之資於耕、衣之資於蠶，而所安所欲之樂在是也，故協極以光其本焉。今觀《無逸》之書、《七月》之詩，帝王所傳心法之要可繹思矣。成王以之致四十年之平，周家以之永八百年之祚，良以敦天下之本，而厚天下之生如是也。
聖制曰：「民之所安所欲者，必首之以衣與食。使無衣無食，未免有凍餓死亡、流離困苦之害。夫匪耕則
translation_en:
…ploughs and ploughshares, and thus the practice of cultivation arose. With cultivation established, the source of food was opened. When Xuanyuan ruled All-under-Heaven, he first taught the people about clothing, and thus the practice of sericulture arose. With sericulture established, the source of clothing was opened. Yao commanded Xi and He to instruct the people in the seasons; Shun commanded Yi and Ji to promote the people’s welfare. Yu and Tang brought order and fostered growth; Wen and Wu brought universal harmony and lasting peace. All followed this Way. Although the Way of the Three Dynasties was fundamentally the same, the institutions of Zhou were especially complete. Thus the Son of Heaven had the ceremony of ploughing the imperial field: one turn and three pushes of the plough [?], with commoners helping to finish the plot. The queen had the ceremony of personally tending silkworms: reeling silk by hand from three basins [?], with the Palace Matrons distributing it in the silkworm palace [?]. The ruler and queen occupied the most exalted positions, yet undertook the toil of the fields. This was because they truly reflected on the hardships of sowing and reaping, and understood that here lay the common people’s livelihood and the foundation of kingly rule. They therefore labored to set an example for All-under-Heaven.
Consequently, the men of that time devoted themselves to cultivation, as expressed in the words, “Attend also to your ploughing, ten thousand working in pairs.” The women devoted themselves to sericulture, as expressed in the words, “The women take up their deep baskets and seek tender mulberry leaves.” Vast though All-under-Heaven was, everyone labored at farming and sericulture. They truly recognized that food depended on cultivation and clothing on silkworms, and that the happiness of enjoying what they found comforting and desirable lay therein. Thus they conformed to the supreme standard and brought distinction to this foundation. If we now examine “Against Idleness” in the Book of Documents and the poem “The Seventh Month” in the Book of Odes, we can reflect upon and discern the essentials of the teaching of the mind transmitted by emperors and kings. Through this, King Cheng achieved forty years of peace, and the house of Zhou prolonged its dynastic tenure to eight hundred years. This was truly because they strengthened the foundations of All-under-Heaven and enriched the people’s livelihood in this way.
The Emperor’s decree reads: “Among the things that give the people comfort and satisfy their desires, clothing and food must come first. Without clothing and food, they cannot escape the afflictions of cold, hunger, death, displacement, and hardship. If there is no cultivation, then …

title: 嘉靖十一年進士登科錄
text:
何以取食弗蠶則何以資衣斯二者亦王者之所
念而憂者也大哉
皇言其真得帝王之法而敦本以厚天下之生者乎
何其憂勤惕勵如此也臣嘗竊觀天下之勢矣
錢鎛在野非不耕也而閭閻猶啼饑之衆杼機
在室非不蠶也而寰宇多號寒之民此其故何
耶漢賈誼告文帝曰一人耕之十人聚而食之
欲天下無饑不可得也十人織之不能衣一人
欲天下無寒不可得也夫誼之為是言也豈無
見於天下之勢而云爾哉盖以天下之物生之
===
===

translation_en:
…how could food be obtained? Without raising silkworms, how could clothing be supplied? These two matters are also what a king keeps in mind and worries over. How great are Your Majesty’s words! Do they not truly grasp the methods of the ancient emperors and kings, strengthening the foundations so as to enrich the livelihood of all under Heaven? How profound are the concern, diligence, vigilance, and resolve they express!

Your servant has ventured to observe conditions throughout the realm. Spades and hoes are in the fields: it is not that people do not cultivate the land. Yet among the common households there are still multitudes crying out in hunger. Shuttles and looms are in the houses: it is not that people do not raise silkworms. Yet throughout the realm many people cry out from cold. Why is this? Jia Yi of the Han told Emperor Wen: “One person tills, and ten gather to eat what he produces. To wish that none under Heaven should go hungry is then to wish for the impossible. Ten people weave, yet cannot clothe one person. To wish that none under Heaven should suffer cold is then to wish for the impossible.” Could Jia Yi have spoken thus without insight into conditions throughout the realm?

For the abundance or failure of what the world produces depends upon Heaven, while the amount consumed depends upon people. Already many people throughout the realm abandon the fundamental occupations to pursue secondary ones, and the idle and indolent account for another half. What those who toil throughout the year produce is insufficient to meet consumption, and superfluous, unproductive people further deplete it. Those of former times who discussed government spoke of official establishments swollen by redundant personnel, salary expenditure swollen by those fed without useful service, and military establishments swollen by unnecessary expense. They also spoke of rewards becoming excessive through indiscriminate grants, customary practices becoming excessive through extravagance, and the pursuit of profit becoming excessive through eagerness to chase it. These two accounts [?] both describe the causes of hunger and cold; Jia Yi’s argument alone does not exhaust them.

When hunger and cold afflict people directly, their cries of resentment and anguished spirits rise to disturb Heaven’s harmony, bringing disasters of flood, drought, and locusts. When the people are displaced and the granaries depleted, foreign peoples watch for opportunities, and the smoke and dust of war arise on the frontiers. When the idle and indolent have no means of support and are hard pressed in every aspect of their livelihood, lawlessness grows daily more unrestrained, and bandits arise within the realm.

聖治於萬一乎我
皇上體元居正通變宜民設施於
九五之尊炳煥於敷天之下者臣得見知於依被之
餘久矣請以是而颺言之而竊以一得之愚附
焉今夫聖人理天下使萬物各得其所為至極
而君相以父母天下為王道故斯民失所則當
敦本以厚天下之生治化未孚則當達權以通
天下之變此帝王善治之規古今不易之法也
punctuated:
聖制曰：「耕者無幾，而食者衆；蠶者甚稀，而衣者多。又加以水旱蝗蟲之為災，游墮冗雜之為害，邊有煙塵，內有盜賊，無怪乎民受其殃日甚一日也。」是陛下之沉幾先物，加志窮民，有以深識天下之勢，而洞見其受弊之源矣。然猶省躬自咎，以上不能參調化機，下不能作興治理，而憂且愧焉。且又以時有今昔，權有通變，欲有道以致雨暘時若，災害不生，百姓足食足衣，力乎農而務乎織，順乎道而歸乎化，惓惓以清問芻蕘之臣焉。是即堯咨衢室、舜察邇言、禹湯不自滿假、文武不敢康寧之誠也。
臣愚，學不足以明理，智不足以識時，抑何以仰裨聖治於萬一乎？我皇上體元居正，通變宜民，設施於九五之尊，炳煥於敷天之下者，臣得見知於依被之餘久矣。請以是而颺言之，而竊以一得之愚附焉。
今夫聖人理天下，使萬物各得其所為至極，而君相以父母天下為王道。故斯民失所，則當敦本以厚天下之生；治化未孚，則當達權以通天下之變。此帝王善治之規，古今不易之法也。
translation_en:
The Emperor's decree reads: “Those who plow are few, while those who eat are many; those who raise silkworms are very scarce, while those who wear clothing are numerous. Added to this are the calamities of floods, droughts, and locusts, and the harm caused by the idle and the superfluous. There is the smoke and dust of warfare on the frontiers and there are bandits within. It is no wonder that the people's suffering grows worse by the day.” This shows that Your Majesty, through profound discernment of incipient developments before events unfold and attentive concern for the impoverished people, deeply understands the condition of the realm and clearly perceives the sources of its afflictions. Yet you still examine yourself and take the blame, anxious and ashamed that, above, you have been unable to assist in harmonizing the workings of cosmic transformation and, below, unable to invigorate good government. Moreover, recognizing that present circumstances differ from those of antiquity and that discretionary measures must adapt to change, you seek a way to bring rain and sunshine in their proper seasons and prevent disasters from arising, so that the common people have sufficient food and clothing, labor at farming and apply themselves to weaving, follow the Way, and submit to moral transformation. With earnest solicitude, you graciously question servants as humble as grass cutters and wood gatherers. This is precisely the sincerity with which Yao sought counsel in the hall at the crossroads, Shun examined the words of those near at hand, Yu and Tang refused to be complacent, and Kings Wen and Wu dared not rest at ease.
Your servant is foolish: my learning is insufficient to comprehend principles, and my wisdom insufficient to understand the times. How, then, could I contribute even the smallest measure to your sagely government? Our August Sovereign embodies the primal principle and occupies his rightful position, adapting to change for the people's benefit. The measures you institute from the exalted sovereign position—the Nine in the Fifth Place—shine brilliantly throughout all beneath Heaven. Your servant, sheltered by your beneficence, has long been able to witness and understand them. Permit me to proclaim these things and humbly append the one insight that even a fool may attain.
Now, when a sage governs the realm, his ultimate aim is to ensure that all things find their proper place; and for the ruler and his chief ministers, the Kingly Way consists in acting as father and mother to all under Heaven. Thus, when the people lose their proper place, one must strengthen the foundations to enrich the livelihood of all under Heaven; when government and moral transformation have not yet won their trust, one must understand discretionary action in order to respond effectively to changes throughout the realm. This is the pattern of good government for emperors and kings, an unchanging rule from antiquity to the present.

translation_en:
Now, speaking of strengthening the foundations: it has long been the case that farming and sericulture have not regained their ancient condition. Our Emperor has gloriously elucidated the Nine Categories of the Great Plan, treasuring sowing and reaping; he has put the Six Storehouses in due order, attaching weight to land and grain. His sacred person takes up the plough in the southern suburbs: this is the ancient ceremony of pushing the plough three times. The Empress personally tends the mulberries in the inner gardens: this is the ancient ceremony of reeling silk three times. Thus the many lords and ministers follow this example below, and agricultural work is diligently pursued; the imperial consorts and palace women of the Six Palaces follow it within, and the rites of sericulture flourish. In strengthening the foundations and setting an example for all under Heaven, he has assuredly already acted in person from his position above.

Speaking, in turn, of adapting to change: abuses inevitably arise when laws have long been in force. Our Emperor’s undivided virtue shines forth and reaches its object, and all institutions are properly ordered. He assists in harmonizing the workings of transformation and promotes orderly government. He reveres Heaven and labors for the people, establishing orderly provisions for prayers and thanksgiving offerings, relief, and loans. He prohibits extravagance and restrains violence, regulating distinctions of rank and prescribed forms, military affairs, and punishments. Thus rites, music, instruction, and moral transformation have all been revived, and those above and below, throughout the four quarters, all wish to purify themselves to receive his beneficent virtue. In exercising discretion to adapt appropriately to change, he has again displayed inspired discernment from above.

Now, strengthening the foundations to enrich the livelihood of all under Heaven should surely bring prosperity to every person’s livelihood. Yet people still cannot escape cold and hunger. Could it be that, although the imperial heart is earnest and compassionate, those charged with carrying out his wishes do not do so in substance? Exercising discretion to accommodate the changes of the world should surely allow changing circumstances to be fully addressed. Yet imbalances and obstructions have still not been remedied. Could it be …

title: 嘉靖十一年進士登科錄
text:
乃
王制雖詳密而化裁者之或有敝乎盖君者出令者
也臣行其令而致之民焉理也君有惠下之德
而臣無宣德之誠則膏屯而靡施斯民安得不
受其殃也政者救時者也時有所極而變生焉
勢也時有可變之勢而吾無神化之方則弊流
而弗返斯治安得而盡其善也是故必奉行之
實而後本可敦也必化裁之當而後變可通也
且力農而務織足食而足衣順道而歸化有生
者之所同欲也今顧有欲耕而無其田有田而
===
不得耕者矣欲蠶而無其桑有桑而不得蠶者
矣又奚望其禮節之知而道化之協也此豈可
責之民耶上恬而下熈內安而外靜時和而沴
消願治者之所樂聞也今邊塵或有鼓之者矣
內寇或有致之者矣而天災時變又未必無所
感也此豈可委之數耶其所以奉而行之化而
裁之亦惟存乎其人而已爾是故奉行之道最
患乎虛名之相尚而實效之無補而化裁之方
則以順時宜民補偏救弊為首務焉然則為之
柰何必也天子以實責宰相宰相以實責監司
