punctuated:
乃王制雖詳密，而化裁者之或有敝乎？盖君者，出令者也；臣行其令而致之民焉，理也。君有惠下之德，而臣無宣德之誠，則膏屯而靡施，斯民安得不受其殃也？政者，救時者也；時有所極而變生焉，勢也。時有可變之勢，而吾無神化之方，則弊流而弗返，斯治安得而盡其善也？是故必奉行之實，而後本可敦也；必化裁之當，而後變可通也。
且力農而務織，足食而足衣，順道而歸化，有生者之所同欲也。今顧有欲耕而無其田，有田而不得耕者矣；欲蠶而無其桑，有桑而不得蠶者矣。又奚望其禮節之知而道化之協也？此豈可責之民耶？上恬而下熈，內安而外靜，時和而沴消，願治者之所樂聞也。今邊塵或有鼓之者矣，內寇或有致之者矣，而天災時變又未必無所感也。此豈可委之數耶？其所以奉而行之、化而裁之，亦惟存乎其人而已爾。是故奉行之道，最患乎虛名之相尚而實效之無補；而化裁之方，則以順時宜民、補偏救弊為首務焉。然則為之柰何？必也天子以實責宰相，宰相以實責監司。
translation_en:
…could it be that, although the sovereign’s institutions are detailed and thorough, those who adapt them to circumstances sometimes introduce defects? The ruler issues commands; his ministers carry them out and bring them to the people. This is the proper order. If the ruler possesses the virtue of benefiting those below, but his ministers lack sincerity in extending that virtue, his bounty accumulates without being distributed. How can the people escape the resulting harm? Government remedies the troubles of its time; when circumstances reach their limit, change arises. This is the natural tendency of affairs. If circumstances permit change, but we lack the means of effecting subtle transformation, abuses will spread unchecked. How, then, can government attain its full excellence? Thus, only with genuine implementation can the foundations be strengthened; only with appropriate adaptation can changing circumstances be successfully addressed.
Moreover, to work diligently at farming and weaving, to have sufficient food and clothing, and to follow the Way and submit to its transforming influence are desires shared by all living people. Yet now there are those who wish to plough but have no land, and those who have land but cannot plough it; those who wish to raise silkworms but have no mulberry trees, and those who have mulberry trees but cannot raise silkworms. How can we further expect them to understand ritual propriety and accord with the transforming influence of the Way? Can the people be blamed for this? Tranquillity above and prosperity below, peace within and quiet beyond the borders, harmonious seasons and the disappearance of baleful influences: these are what those who desire good government delight to hear of. Yet now there may be those who stir up the dust of warfare on the frontiers, and those who bring about banditry within the realm. Natural disasters and untimely anomalies, too, may well have something that calls them forth. Can these things be left to fate? The means of carrying out commands and adapting institutions depend solely upon the people entrusted with them. Thus, in implementation, the greatest danger is mutual esteem for empty reputation without any beneficial practical results. In adaptation, the foremost tasks are to accord with the times, benefit the people, correct imbalances, and remedy abuses. How, then, should this be done? The Son of Heaven must demand substantive results from the chief councillors, and the chief councillors must demand substantive results from the surveillance commissioners…

title: 嘉靖十一年進士登科錄
text:
監司以實責守令守令以實責庶民而後謂之
奉行之實必也仰以觀于天文俯以察于地理
中以觀于人物遠以稽于先王近以酌于時政
而後謂之化裁之宜故為今之計不徒彌文之
是飾也而必尚實以敦其本焉不貴更張之無
漸也而必達權以通其變焉閭閻有勸課之吏
末作嚴裁抑之防工役罷不急之務賦斂禁催
科之擾豪強抑兼併之習而又去三浮以從實
酌三盈以從約則民將力乎農而務乎織而衣
食無不足之患矣郡邑有循良之吏鄉里弘庠
===
塾之規力田敦孝弟之懿士習崇禮義之正本
俗無緇黃之惑而又修五禮以防偽明七政以
齊民則人將歸乎道而順乎化而游墮冗雜之
不為害矣由是練勇敢勵戰鬭旌才略以務治
軍選將之實而又篤周之采薇以下五詩之義
焉則邊疆有吉甫方叔之將而煙塵可息矣由
是察言行課功狀公薦舉以務求賢審官之實
而又如漢之重二千石之義焉則郡邑有龔黃
卓魯之賢而盜賊可化矣至于欲雨暘時若而
災害之不生則又在

punctuated: 監司以實責守令，守令以實責庶民，而後謂之奉行之實。必也仰以觀于天文，俯以察于地理，中以觀于人物，遠以稽于先王，近以酌于時政，而後謂之化裁之宜。故為今之計，不徒彌文之是飾也，而必尚實以敦其本焉；不貴更張之無漸也，而必達權以通其變焉。閭閻有勸課之吏，末作嚴裁抑之防，工役罷不急之務，賦斂禁催科之擾，豪強抑兼併之習，而又去三浮以從實，酌三盈以從約，則民將力乎農而務乎織，而衣食無不足之患矣。郡邑有循良之吏，鄉里弘庠塾之規，力田敦孝弟之懿，士習崇禮義之正，本俗無緇黃之惑，而又修五禮以防偽，明七政以齊民，則人將歸乎道而順乎化，而游墮冗雜之不為害矣。由是練勇敢，勵戰鬭，旌才略，以務治軍選將之實，而又篤周之《采薇》以下五詩之義焉，則邊疆有吉甫、方叔之將，而煙塵可息矣。由是察言行，課功狀，公薦舉，以務求賢審官之實，而又如漢之重二千石之義焉，則郡邑有龔、黃、卓、魯之賢，而盜賊可化矣。至于欲雨暘時若而災害之不生，則又在
translation_en:
…the surveillance commissioners must hold prefects and magistrates accountable for concrete results, and prefects and magistrates must hold the common people accountable for concrete results. Only then can this be called genuine implementation. One must look upward to observe celestial patterns, downward to examine the configuration of the earth, and between them to observe people and things; look back to investigate the former kings, and consider current affairs close at hand. Only then can adaptation be called appropriate. Thus, in planning for the present, we must not merely embellish elaborate formalities, but esteem substance to strengthen the foundations; we must not prize changes made without gradual steps, but understand discretionary judgment so as to respond to changing circumstances.

Let there be officials among the people who encourage and oversee productive work; strictly enforce restraints on secondary occupations; discontinue nonurgent construction and labor services; prohibit harassment in the collection of taxes; and curb the powerful families’ practice of engrossing land. Moreover, eliminate the “three extravagances” in favor of substance, and moderate the “three excesses” in favor of economy. Then the people will devote their strength to farming and apply themselves to weaving, and there will be no danger of insufficient clothing and food.

Let prefectures and counties have conscientious and benevolent officials; extend the institutions of local schools throughout the villages; encourage diligent farming and strengthen the virtues of filial piety and fraternal respect; and foster proper ritual conduct and righteousness among scholars. Let local customs [?] be free from the delusions of Buddhist monks and Daoist priests. Moreover, cultivate the five categories of rites to guard against deceit, and clarify the seven celestial regulators to bring order to the people. Then people will return to the Way and follow moral instruction, and idle, indolent, superfluous, and miscellaneous elements will cause no harm.

On this basis, train the brave, encourage fighting spirit, and honor ability and strategy, thereby pursuing concrete results in managing armies and selecting generals. Further, earnestly uphold the meaning of the five Zhou poems beginning with Gathering Ferns (Caiwei). Then the frontiers will have generals like Jifu and Fang Shu, and the smoke and dust of warfare can subside. On this basis, examine words and conduct, assess records of achievement, and make recommendations impartially, thereby pursuing concrete results in seeking worthy men and scrutinizing appointments. Further, follow the Han principle of attaching great importance to officials ranked at two thousand bushels. Then prefectures and counties will have worthy officials like Gong, Huang, Zhuo, and Lu, and bandits can be reformed. As for wishing rain and sunshine to come in their proper seasons and disasters not to arise, that further depends upon…

title: 嘉靖十一年進士登科錄
text:
聖天子建中和之極臻位育之功而凡諸臣同心協
德興道致治三孤以調燮鼎鼐無娼嫉私刻之
流六卿以贊襄機務無險詖傾側之士有官守
者盡其職而不曠厥工有言責者盡其忠而不
愧厥職有功必賞有罪必罰俾體統正而
朝廷尊有利必興有害必除俾恩惠流而教化廣
由是人事盡於下而天變自回人心和於上而
天休自至將見穹靈錫祐壤祇貢祉山出器車
河出馬圖至治馨香達于神明協氣氤氳盈于
宇宙
===
前星炳耀百男兆麟趾之祥
後祿延和萬國鞏鴻圖之運所謂天德孚而王道
成者蓋至矣盛矣而無以加矣易曰唯深也故
能通天下之志唯幾也故能成天下之務唯神
也故不疾而速不行而至臣草野之人不識忌
諱謹以是為
聖明獻臣無任殞越之至臣謹對

也故不疾而速不行而至臣草野之人不識忌
諱謹以是為
聖明獻臣無任殞越之至臣謹對
punctuated: 聖天子建中和之極，臻位育之功，而凡諸臣同心協德，興道致治。三孤以調燮鼎鼐，無娼嫉私刻之流；六卿以贊襄機務，無險詖傾側之士。有官守者盡其職而不曠厥工，有言責者盡其忠而不愧厥職。有功必賞，有罪必罰，俾體統正而朝廷尊；有利必興，有害必除，俾恩惠流而教化廣。由是人事盡於下而天變自回，人心和於上而天休自至。將見穹靈錫祐，壤祇貢祉，山出器車，河出馬圖，至治馨香達于神明，協氣氤氳盈于宇宙。前星炳耀，百男兆麟趾之祥；後祿延和，萬國鞏鴻圖之運。所謂天德孚而王道成者，蓋至矣，盛矣，而無以加矣！《易》曰：「唯深也，故能通天下之志；唯幾也，故能成天下之務；唯神也，故不疾而速，不行而至。」臣草野之人，不識忌諱，謹以是為聖明獻。臣無任殞越之至，臣謹對。
translation_en:
…the sagely Son of Heaven establishing the supreme standard of equilibrium and harmony, bringing heaven and earth to their proper places and all things to their full development, while all his ministers unite in purpose and virtue to advance the Way and achieve good government. Let the Three Junior Preceptors harmonize affairs of state, as one blends the contents of the sacrificial cauldrons, with none among them given to jealousy [?], selfishness, or harshness. Let the Six Ministers assist in crucial affairs, with none among them treacherous, biased, or devious. Let those holding office fulfill their duties without neglecting their work, and those charged with remonstrance give their utmost loyalty without disgracing their responsibilities. Merit must invariably be rewarded and wrongdoing punished, so that the proper hierarchy is maintained and the court commands respect. Whatever is beneficial must be promoted and whatever is harmful removed, so that beneficence spreads and moral instruction reaches far and wide.
Thus, when human responsibilities are fully discharged below, Heaven’s portents will naturally abate; when people’s hearts are brought into harmony above, Heaven’s blessings will naturally arrive. We shall then see the spirits of Heaven bestow protection and the deities of Earth offer blessings; mountains will bring forth wondrous chariots [?], and the river will yield the horse bearing the Chart. The fragrance of perfect government will reach the spirits, and harmonious vital forces will suffuse the universe. The Foremost Star, signifying the heir apparent, will shine brightly, and a hundred sons will herald the auspicious promise of “The Qilin’s Hoofs.” Blessings for posterity will perpetuate harmony [?], and the myriad states will secure the enduring fortunes of the grand imperial enterprise. What is called making Heaven’s virtue manifest and bringing the Kingly Way to fulfillment will surely have reached its utmost perfection and splendor, beyond which nothing can be added!
The Book of Changes says: “Only through profundity can one comprehend the aspirations of all under Heaven; only through discerning the incipient can one accomplish the affairs of all under Heaven; only through spiritual efficacy can one be swift without haste and arrive without traveling.” Your servant is a man of the countryside, ignorant of taboos. I respectfully offer these words to Your Sagely Majesty. Your servant is overwhelmed with trepidation. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

title: 嘉靖十一年進士登科錄
text:
臣高節
臣對臣聞天下有不可易之法而率之存乎心
天下無不可化之民而動之存乎機何則法以
致理凡可以監古者無復能易也而耕蠶於日
用為尤切然所以基之者心焉耳矣是心者率
法之基也民以順應凡可以轉移者無復難施
也而農桑於民用為尤急然所以感之者機焉
耳矣是機也者又所以立民之感也夫惟基固
而後可以為循法之本感立而後可以責民心
之應其或基不先定則志奪於習俗之故用梏
===
於時勢之殊而其失也為無斷感不能誠則上
不足以神變化之道下不足以通天下之志而
其失也為徒法二者之失形而因循之弊錮則
政日以怠志日以惰而天下之大計荒矣如斯
世斯民何是故心存則神智精明而帝王之法
張矣機立則變通宜民而玩愒之氣作矣法張
而舉世皆有持循據守之方氣作而天下盡化
為歌詠勤苦之俗將見上得以享豐亨豫大之
樂下得以遂飽煖安樂之願協氣嘉生薫為太
和而誦聲四作泰道一新尚何災沴之足虞哉

punctuated:
臣高節。

臣對：臣聞天下有不可易之法，而率之存乎心；天下無不可化之民，而動之存乎機。何則？法以致理，凡可以監古者，無復能易也，而耕蠶於日用為尤切；然所以基之者，心焉耳矣。是心者，率法之基也。民以順應，凡可以轉移者，無復難施也，而農桑於民用為尤急；然所以感之者，機焉耳矣。是機也者，又所以立民之感也。夫惟基固，而後可以為循法之本；感立，而後可以責民心之應。其或基不先定，則志奪於習俗之故，用梏於時勢之殊，而其失也為無斷；感不能誠，則上不足以神變化之道，下不足以通天下之志，而其失也為徒法。二者之失形，而因循之弊錮，則政日以怠，志日以惰，而天下之大計荒矣。如斯世斯民何？是故心存，則神智精明，而帝王之法張矣；機立，則變通宜民，而玩愒之氣作矣。法張，而舉世皆有持循據守之方；氣作，而天下盡化為歌詠勤苦之俗。將見上得以享豐亨豫大之樂，下得以遂飽煖安樂之願，協氣嘉生，薫為太和，而誦聲四作，泰道一新，尚何災沴之足虞哉！
translation_en:
Your servant Gao Jie.

Your servant replies: I have heard that there are immutable institutions in the realm, but following them depends upon the heart; there are no people in the realm incapable of transformation, but stirring them depends upon the activating impulse. Why is this? Institutions bring about good order. Whatever can serve to take antiquity as a model admits of no alteration, and plowing and silkworm raising are especially pertinent to daily life. Yet what provides their foundation is simply the heart. The heart is thus the foundation for following institutions. The people respond compliantly: whatever can bring about their transformation is not difficult to implement, and agriculture and sericulture are especially urgent for their livelihood. Yet what moves them is simply the activating impulse. This impulse is what establishes the people's responsiveness.

Only when the foundation is firm can there be a basis for following institutions; only when responsiveness is established can a response be expected from the people's hearts. If the foundation is not first secured, the will is overpowered by established customs, and its exercise is fettered by differing circumstances; the resulting fault is indecision. If the influence exerted cannot be sincere, it is insufficient, above, to make the way of transformation divinely efficacious and, below, to comprehend the aspirations of all under Heaven; the resulting fault is institutions existing in name alone. When these two faults emerge and the abuse of merely following precedent becomes entrenched, government grows daily more negligent, resolve daily more indolent, and the great undertakings of the realm fall into neglect. What, then, can be done for this age and its people?

Thus, when the heart remains attentive, spiritual perception and understanding become keen and clear, and the institutions of emperors and kings flourish. When the activating impulse is established, adaptation benefits the people, and the spirit of idle procrastination is roused to action [?]. When institutions flourish, everyone has principles to follow and uphold; when their spirits are roused, all under Heaven adopt the custom of singing in praise of diligent toil. We shall then see those above enjoying the pleasures of abundance, prosperity, ease, and greatness, and those below fulfilling their wishes for sufficient food and warmth, security and happiness. Harmonious vital forces and flourishing living things will blend into supreme harmony; voices of praise will rise on every side, and the way of peace and prosperity will be wholly renewed. What calamities or malign influences would then be worth fearing?

title: 嘉靖十一年進士登科錄
text:
此固古昔聖帝明王已試之明驗而詩書之所
紀載者也欽惟
皇帝陛下承天心發大業軫民生衣食之源舉帝王
耕蠶之典天下固已回心而嚮道樂事而勸功
矣乃復
不自神聖清問下及臣愚知
陛下此心即堯舜禹湯文武憂勤惕厲之心也倡率
化道之機盖已潜孚默應乎四方萬國之遠而

This is indeed clear evidence already tested by the sage emperors and enlightened kings of antiquity and recorded in the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents. I reverently reflect that Your Majesty the Emperor has accorded with Heaven’s mind and initiated great undertakings, shown concern for the sources of the people’s food and clothing, and performed the imperial rites of ploughing and sericulture. All under Heaven have already turned their hearts toward the Way, taken pleasure in their tasks, and exerted themselves in their work. Yet, without presuming upon your own divine sagacity, you have further extended your august inquiry down to us. Foolish though I am, I know that this concern of Your Majesty is precisely the anxious diligence and vigilant self-discipline of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu. The impulse by which you lead through example and guide through transformation has surely already won an unseen trust and silent response even in the distant lands of the four quarters and the myriad states. It also accords with the essentials of the teaching of the mind transmitted across countless generations. Yet your sagely purpose remains humble, as though something still leaves you uneasy. You therefore consult even grass-cutters and wood-gatherers, weighing antiquity against the evidence of the present, intending to bring all the people and living things of this age into a realm of benevolence and longevity. This is a matter of the utmost consequence for human life. Though foolish and unlearned, how could I dare not gather what I have heard and offer it to you? May Your divine sagacity select what is worthy.
I have heard that, when government was discussed at the court of Yu, it was said: “Virtue finds expression in good government; government consists in nourishing the people.” Accordingly, rectifying virtue, facilitating the use of resources, and enriching livelihoods were brought into harmony, while water, fire, metal, wood, earth, and grain were properly managed. At the height of its flourishing, these six resources and three duties were indeed well ordered. Fearing that this might not endure, they further encouraged their practice through the Nine Songs, so that they would not fall into decay. The flourishing Zhou established its state upon agriculture and sericulture. Thus the Duke of Zhou’s admonition in “Against Idleness” (Wu yi), and the poems “The Sixth Month” (Liu yue) and “The Seventh Month” (Qi yue), repeatedly dwell upon the movements of the sun, moon, and stars, the transformations of insects, plants, and trees, and the proper seasons for preparing ploughshares, setting feet to work in the fields, sowing grain, and clearing the threshing ground, using these to admonish King Cheng…

title: 嘉靖十一年進士登科錄
text:
焉嗚呼治至虞周可謂極矣而其所以為民者
惟生養是先蓋以其切於民命焉耳及其衰也
舍我穡事之怨興而四海始困窮矣不籍千畝
而鴻鴈哀鳴之聲作矣夫同是天下則所以率
先之者不容以頓異同是民心則所以倡道之
者豈容於頓殊此雖時勢之變更良由世主失
所操持之所致也是故漢文作而勸農親蠶之
儀舉則海內致殷富之盛唐宗起而力行仁義
之道至則庶幾並成康之勳彼徒求諸法而弗
求諸心尚得以擅英君誼辟之名而況得帝王
===
心法感通之本者哉夫今之天下即古之天下
然則古人之道今獨不可復乎而況夫人心虛
靈不昧之體應務不窮之用感昭神化之方達
權倡率之妙雖堯舜亦與人同也而謂操可致
之權又有能致之資者可安常習故而漫弗之
省乎此愚臣所嘗究觀往籍而扼腕弗平者也
伏惟
陛下超然遠覽洞燭民艱每歲循耕籍之典所以率
天下者何其勤
大內嚴躬桑之儀所以風天下者何其備則

焉。嗚呼！治至虞周，可謂極矣，而其所以為民者，惟生養是先，蓋以其切於民命焉耳。及其衰也，「舍我穡事」之怨興，而四海始困窮矣；不籍千畝，而鴻鴈哀鳴之聲作矣。夫同是天下，則所以率先之者，不容以頓異；同是民心，則所以倡道之者，豈容於頓殊？此雖時勢之變更，良由世主失所操持之所致也。是故漢文作，而勸農親蠶之儀舉，則海內致殷富之盛；唐宗起，而力行仁義之道至，則庶幾並成康之勳。彼徒求諸法，而弗求諸心，尚得以擅英君誼辟之名，而況得帝王心法感通之本者哉！

…to him. Alas! Government under Yu and Zhou may be called the highest attainment, yet in all they did for the people, they gave priority to sustaining and nourishing them, precisely because these matters directly concerned the people's lives. When their rule declined, resentment arose at “abandoning our work in the fields,” and all within the Four Seas began to suffer poverty and distress. When the thousand-mu ceremonial field was left untilled, the plaintive cries of wild geese arose. The realm remained the same: how could the means of leading it by example suddenly become wholly different? The people's hearts remained the same: how could the means of guiding them suddenly change altogether? Although circumstances had changed, this was truly the consequence of rulers losing their hold upon what they should have maintained. Thus, when Emperor Wen of Han arose and instituted ceremonies encouraging agriculture and personally tending silkworms, the realm attained great prosperity. When the Tang sovereign arose and devoted himself fully to practicing benevolence and righteousness, his achievements nearly equaled those of Kings Cheng and Kang. They sought merely in methods, without seeking in the heart, yet still won renown as outstanding sovereigns and righteous rulers. How much more could one accomplish who grasped the foundation of moral influence and responsiveness in the teachings of the ancient emperors and kings concerning the heart!
The realm today is the realm of antiquity. Can the Way of the ancients alone be impossible to restore today? Moreover, the heart's essential nature—empty, numinously perceptive, and unobscured—its inexhaustible capacity to respond to affairs, its means of exerting an illuminating influence and bringing about spiritual transformation, and its subtle ability to adapt to circumstances and lead by example: in these, even Yao and Shun were no different from other people. Can it then be said that someone who holds the authority to achieve these ends and possesses the capacity to do so may remain content with customary practices and old habits, carelessly failing to examine them? These are the matters that, whenever your ignorant servant has closely studied the records of the past, have made him wring his hands in dismay.
I humbly consider that Your Majesty surveys matters with transcendent breadth and fully perceives the people's hardships. Each year you observe the rite of plowing the ceremonial field: how diligently you lead the realm by example! 陛下之心上有以契千聖之奥而道民之機下有以
警萬國之心是宜閭閻極儲峙之豐井落臻盈
篚之帛内寧外謐災沴殄銷也夫何邇年以来
關輔告歉則不免發内帑之積枹鼓時警則不
能施賑貸之策或者
聖心猶有未純而其機尚有阻勸乎然臣觀
陛下閔念黎元頻切
詔㫖仰稽之天則靈雪寳露降焉俯察之地則瑞
麥嘉禾出焉中驗之人心則訢訢然浹

===

而感格倡率之機又以昭布寰宇未可謂其弗

能精白一心以承

title: 嘉靖十一年進士登科錄
text:
班內外咸共其事不必躬履田畝而天下化矣
后以率夫人世婦以及士庶人之妻而天下則
焉則天下不必家喻而亦化之矣此古昔聖帝
明王所以高拱於清穆之上而化行於海隅之
遠者以其有此具也今也勸農之吏雖設而尸
素以得計曾有如禹之乘四載以服勤於舜者
乎而况遼邈之邑監司所不能按者抑又多矣
民生之食如之何其弗歉也剥削之苦又所不
計矣植桑之園猶故而别業以自利曾有如詩
人刺蠶織之休以冀復周制者乎而况綺羅之
===
===
輩所以肆誅求乎吾民者又無紀極矣民生之
衣如之何其不鶉結也瑣尾之痛又有所不忍
言矣是皆不知小人之依安保其有寅亮之心
哉夫維昔之富不如時維今之疚不若兹周人
所以嘆家法之失也大東小東杼軸其空周詩
所以怨征求之苦也以今考古是安得不上廑
淵衷下究化理哉昔真德秀著田家之苦以規其
君有所謂曉霜未釋忍飢扶犂凍皴不可忍則
燎草火以自温者為始耕之苦焉燠氣將炎晨
興以出傴僂如啄至夕乃休泥塗被體熱爍濕

班，內外咸共其事，不必躬履田畝而天下化矣。后以率夫人、世婦以及士庶人之妻，而天下則焉，則天下不必家喻而亦化之矣。此古昔聖帝明王所以高拱於清穆之上，而化行於海隅之遠者，以其有此具也。今也，勸農之吏雖設，而尸素以得計，曾有如禹之乘四載以服勤於舜者乎？而况遼邈之邑，監司所不能按者，抑又多矣。民生之食，如之何其弗歉也？剥削之苦，又所不計矣。植桑之園猶故，而别業以自利，曾有如詩人刺蠶織之休，以冀復周制者乎？而况綺羅之輩，所以肆誅求乎吾民者，又無紀極矣。民生之衣，如之何其不鶉結也？瑣尾之痛，又有所不忍言矣。是皆不知小人之依，安保其有寅亮之心哉？

夫「維昔之富，不如時；維今之疚，不若兹」，周人所以嘆家法之失也。「大東小東，杼軸其空」，周詩所以怨征求之苦也。以今考古，是安得不上廑淵衷，下究化理哉？

昔真德秀著田家之苦，以規其君，有所謂曉霜未釋，忍飢扶犂，凍皴不可忍，則燎草火以自温者，為始耕之苦焉。燠氣將炎，晨興以出，傴僂如啄，至夕乃休，泥塗被體，熱爍濕
translation_en:
…according to their ranks, all within and without shared in the work. There was no need for the sovereign personally to tread the fields for all under Heaven to be transformed. The queen led the palace consorts and women of the hereditary households, down to the wives of gentlemen and commoners, and all under Heaven followed their example. Thus, without instruction reaching each household individually, all under Heaven were likewise transformed. The sage emperors and enlightened kings of antiquity could sit on high with folded hands in serene dignity, while their transforming influence reached the distant shores, because they possessed these means. Today, although officials charged with encouraging agriculture have been appointed, they regard drawing salaries without performing their duties as a successful strategy. Has there been anyone like Yu, who used four kinds of conveyance to labor diligently in Shun’s service? Moreover, there are many remote districts that the regional surveillance officials cannot inspect. How could the people’s food supplies fail to fall short? This does not even reckon the suffering caused by extortion. The mulberry gardens remain as before, yet other occupations are pursued for private gain. Has there been anyone like the poet who censured the abandonment of sericulture and weaving, hoping to restore the institutions of Zhou? Moreover, those clad in fine silks impose demands upon our people without any restraint or limit. How could the people’s clothing fail to become knotted rags, like a quail’s patchy plumage? The pain of their abject distress is more than one can bear to describe. These officials all fail to understand what the common people depend upon. How can we be sure that they have a heart to assist their sovereign with reverence?

The words, “The prosperity of former days was not like that of this time; the suffering of today was not like this” [?], express how the people of Zhou lamented the loss of their ancestral institutions. “In the greater east and the lesser east, the looms stand empty”: this Zhou poem voices resentment at the suffering caused by exactions. Comparing the present with antiquity, how could these matters fail to trouble Your Majesty’s profound heart above, and prompt a thorough inquiry into the principles of transforming government below?

Formerly, Zhen Dexiu wrote of the hardships of farming households to admonish his ruler. He described how, before the morning frost had melted, they endured hunger as they guided the plow; when the freezing and cracking of their skin became unbearable, they burned grass to warm themselves. Such were the hardships of beginning the plowing. As the warmth was about to become intense heat, they rose at dawn and went out, stooping like pecking birds, resting only at evening, their bodies covered in mud, scorched by heat and damp…

title: 嘉靖十一年進士登科錄
text:
蒸百畝告青而形容變化不可復識者為立苗
之苦焉暑日如金田水若沸耘耔是力稂莠是
除爬沙而指為之戾傴僂而腰為之折者為耘
苗之苦焉迨垂穎堅粟則縛草為舍荷戟防衛
竟夜風雨焦勞不輟者為守禾之苦焉登場屬
飽償貸不支則又稱貸嗣歲自此惟取茅以為
生息而蠶事之苦稱是焉嗚呼盡之矣夫民終
歲勤苦若此而啼饑尚不免焉士大夫知此者
鮮矣况貴戚近倖乎無惑乎民生之未安也誠
使奉法者皆能上體
===
聖懷下悉民隱易田必求趙過之智而不憚於循行
繰絲必稽吳中之詠而不使其稱貸監司申飭
乎守令守令必躬乎民畝則天下皆能以聖人
之心為心而風聲所樹無煩刑驅孰不為敦本
務實之圖哉此蓋轉貧為富之機易危為安之
策在
陛下奮乾剛以振天下怠緩之心極明作以起天下
委靡之氣耳夫法無不可行者有所不行以人
心之弗誠也心無不可挽者有所未孚以流俗
之染深也今承積弊之後苟小大戮力上下勩

punctuated: 蒸，百畝告青，而形容變化不可復識者，為立苗之苦焉。暑日如金，田水若沸，耘耔是力，稂莠是除，爬沙而指為之戾，傴僂而腰為之折者，為耘苗之苦焉。迨垂穎堅粟，則縛草為舍，荷戟防衛，竟夜風雨，焦勞不輟者，為守禾之苦焉。登場屬飽，償貸不支，則又稱貸嗣歲，自此惟取茅以為生息，而蠶事之苦稱是焉。嗚呼！盡之矣！夫民終歲勤苦若此，而啼饑尚不免焉。士大夫知此者鮮矣，况貴戚近倖乎？無惑乎民生之未安也！誠使奉法者皆能上體聖懷，下悉民隱，易田必求趙過之智，而不憚於循行；繰絲必稽吳中之詠，而不使其稱貸；監司申飭乎守令，守令必躬乎民畝，則天下皆能以聖人之心為心，而風聲所樹，無煩刑驅，孰不為敦本務實之圖哉？此蓋轉貧為富之機，易危為安之策，在陛下奮乾剛以振天下怠緩之心，極明作以起天下委靡之氣耳。夫法無不可行者，有所不行，以人心之弗誠也；心無不可挽者，有所未孚，以流俗之染深也。今承積弊之後，苟小大戮力，上下勩
translation_en:
…steamed by the damp, until the hundred mu of fields turn green and their appearance has changed beyond recognition: these are the hardships of establishing the seedlings. When the summer sun is like molten metal and the water in the fields seems to boil, they devote their strength to weeding and banking earth around the plants, removing weeds and wild grasses. Scrabbling in the sand twists their fingers; stooping bends their backs to the breaking point: these are the hardships of weeding the seedlings. When the ears droop and the grain hardens, they bind grass into shelters and carry halberds to guard the crop. Through nights of wind and rain, their anxious toil never ceases: these are the hardships of guarding the grain. When the harvest reaches the threshing ground, they have scarcely had enough to eat before repayment of their loans leaves them without sufficient means. They must borrow again for the following year, and thereafter sustain their livelihood only by gathering thatch [?]. The hardships of silkworm raising are comparable. Alas! This exhausts the account!

The people toil bitterly throughout the year in this way, yet still cannot escape crying out in hunger. Few scholar-officials understand this, much less imperial relatives and favored courtiers. No wonder the people's livelihood remains insecure! If only those who administer the laws could all comprehend Your Majesty's intentions above and fully understand the people's hidden sufferings below! In changing cultivation practices [?], they must seek wisdom like Zhao Guo's and not shrink from making inspection tours; concerning silk reeling, they must consult the verses from Wuzhong and ensure that the people need not borrow. The regional surveillance officials should admonish the prefects and magistrates, and the prefects and magistrates must personally visit the people's fields. Then all under Heaven could take the sage's heart as their own. With such an example and influence established, there would be no need to drive them with punishments: who would fail to devise ways to strengthen the agricultural foundation and attend to practical needs?

This is surely the means of turning poverty into wealth and the policy for changing peril into security. It rests solely with Your Majesty to exert the vigorous firmness of Heaven to rouse the indolent hearts of all under Heaven, and to exercise enlightened action to the utmost to revive their dispirited energies. No law is incapable of implementation; where laws go unenforced, it is because people's hearts lack sincerity. No heart is beyond being turned around; where confidence has not yet been won, it is because prevailing customs have exerted too deep an influence. Now, inheriting the consequences of accumulated abuses, if those great and small would join their efforts, and those above and below toil…

title: 嘉靖十一年進士登科錄
text:
恆以虞周之治為必可復以先王之法為必可
行不狃於因仍苟且之見不撓於古今時勢之
殊則法立而功奏事舉而效見何民生衣食之
不充何國用儲積之弗贍民心由是而可醇兵
食由是而可足至治馨香徹於神明和氣薰蒸
天地交泰而雨暘自以時至邊陲自以守固矣
又何用上嘉下樂遠慕近法以勞為哉雖然法
以心率者也機以心神者也是故虞廷每嚴於
危微精一之訓而勑天之命亦必曰惟時惟幾
焉不獨其政在養民已也周公亦致警于所其
===
無逸之戒而後豳風之詩使瞽矇誦焉不徒俾
其知稼穡艱難已也夫心而曰精則所以察之
者密矣無逸而必曰所焉則所以宅心者嚴矣
是故其要存乎幾微之審也不然則心或不免
於外誘之移臣懼法因以隳而機因以弛也臣
愚仰見
陛下德嚴敬一則古人所謂惟敬可以檢束此心者
亦既優為之矣
日御講筵則古人所謂惟學可以養此心者亦既
優為之矣儒紳

punctuated:
恆以虞周之治為必可復，以先王之法為必可行，不狃於因仍苟且之見，不撓於古今時勢之殊，則法立而功奏，事舉而效見。何民生衣食之不充？何國用儲積之弗贍？民心由是而可醇，兵食由是而可足。至治馨香，徹於神明；和氣薰蒸，天地交泰，而雨暘自以時至，邊陲自以守固矣。又何用上嘉下樂、遠慕近法以勞為哉？雖然，法以心率者也，機以心神者也。是故虞廷每嚴於危微精一之訓，而勑天之命亦必曰「惟時惟幾」焉，不獨其政在養民已也。周公亦致警于「所其無逸」之戒，而後《豳風》之詩使瞽矇誦焉，不徒俾其知稼穡艱難已也。夫心而曰精，則所以察之者密矣；無逸而必曰所焉，則所以宅心者嚴矣。是故其要存乎幾微之審也。不然，則心或不免於外誘之移，臣懼法因以隳而機因以弛也。
臣愚仰見陛下德嚴敬一，則古人所謂「惟敬可以檢束此心」者，亦既優為之矣；日御講筵，則古人所謂「惟學可以養此心」者，亦既優為之矣；儒紳
translation_en:
…constantly regard the good government of Yu and Zhou as certainly recoverable, and the laws of the former kings as certainly practicable. If we remain neither bound by notions of merely carrying on and making do, nor deterred by differences between ancient and present circumstances, then laws will be established and achievements realized; undertakings will proceed and results appear. How could the people's clothing and food be insufficient? How could reserves for state expenditure be inadequate? The people's hearts can thereby become sincere, and military provisions become ample. The fragrance of perfect government will reach the spirits; harmonious influences will spread abundantly, and Heaven and Earth will enter into concord. Rain and sunshine will naturally arrive in season, and the frontiers will naturally be securely defended. What need would there then be to toil over winning commendation above and delight below, admiration from afar and emulation nearby?
Nevertheless, laws are guided by the heart, and incipient opportunities are given their subtle efficacy by the heart. Thus the court of Yu always strictly upheld the teaching that the human heart is precarious and the moral heart subtle, and that one must be discerning and single-minded. The injunction to attend reverently to Heaven's commands likewise necessarily said, “Attend to the times and to the first stirrings.” Its government did not consist solely in nourishing the people. The Duke of Zhou likewise sounded a warning in the admonition to “take freedom from ease as one's dwelling”; thereafter he had the blind musicians recite the poems of the Airs of Bin. This was not merely to make the ruler understand the hardships of sowing and reaping. When discernment is prescribed for the heart, the means of examining it must be meticulous. When freedom from ease is specifically called a “dwelling,” the discipline by which the heart is settled must be strict. Thus the essential point lies in scrutinizing the slightest beginnings. Otherwise, the heart may fail to escape being swayed by external temptations. Your servant fears that laws would consequently fall into ruin and opportunities consequently be neglected.
In my humble judgment, I see that Your Majesty's virtue is rigorous in reverence and singleness of purpose. You have therefore already amply fulfilled what the ancients meant by saying, “Only reverence can hold this heart in check.” You attend the Classics Colloquium daily, and have therefore already amply fulfilled what the ancients meant by saying, “Only learning can nourish this heart.” The scholarly officials…

title: 嘉靖十一年進士登科錄
text:
列侍則古人所謂惟親賢人君子可以維持此心
者亦既優為之矣而臣愚之深憂過計竊願
陛下尤致審於幾微焉誠以心體至微衆欲攻之一
或不審則投間抵隙必將為是心之累矣盖事
未有不始於微而成於著者司馬光曰聖人之
慮遠故能謹其微胡寅亦曰善為天下國家者
每謹於微而已矣皆言幾微之不可忽也周敦
頤則指其本曰寂然不動者誠也感而遂通者
神也動而未形有無之間者幾也盖是幾之微
近則公私邪正遠則廢興存亡皆於是乎判焉
===
不可以弗之審也是故誠神幾則聖矣臣願
陛下宫闈深邃之中
心氣清明之時致研於理欲絲毫之分考驗於古
今得失之監不顯亦臨也無射亦保也敬畏崇
焉逸欲戒焉敦朴發自由中儉素本諸天性由
是以循法則法可弘於往聖由是以道民則民
可孚於至愚凡所以為休養生息之方以極博
厚高明之業者自可運諸此心而無難矣臣愚
不勝惓惓之至臣謹對

punctuated:
列侍，則古人所謂「惟親賢人君子可以維持此心」者，亦既優為之矣。而臣愚之深憂過計，竊願陛下尤致審於幾微焉。誠以心體至微，衆欲攻之，一或不審，則投間抵隙，必將為是心之累矣。盖事未有不始於微而成於著者。司馬光曰：「聖人之慮遠，故能謹其微。」胡寅亦曰：「善為天下國家者，每謹於微而已矣。」皆言幾微之不可忽也。周敦頤則指其本曰：「寂然不動者，誠也；感而遂通者，神也；動而未形、有無之間者，幾也。」盖是幾之微，近則公私邪正，遠則廢興存亡，皆於是乎判焉，不可以弗之審也。是故誠、神、幾，則聖矣。
臣願陛下宫闈深邃之中，心氣清明之時，致研於理欲絲毫之分，考驗於古今得失之監。「不顯亦臨」也，「無射亦保」也。敬畏崇焉，逸欲戒焉，敦朴發自由中，儉素本諸天性。由是以循法，則法可弘於往聖；由是以道民，則民可孚於至愚。凡所以為休養生息之方，以極博厚高明之業者，自可運諸此心而無難矣。臣愚不勝惓惓之至，臣謹對。
translation_en:
…stand in attendance, so what the ancients called “sustaining this mind only by drawing close to worthy men and gentlemen” Your Majesty has also already accomplished abundantly. Yet in my foolishness, with deep anxiety and perhaps excessive concern, I humbly wish that Your Majesty would give particular scrutiny to the subtlest beginnings of things. For the substance of the mind is exceedingly subtle, and manifold desires assail it. If scrutiny lapses even once, they will seize an opening and penetrate a gap, inevitably burdening this mind. Nothing fails to begin in the imperceptible and develop into the manifest. Sima Guang said: “The sage’s deliberations reach far; thus he can be watchful over subtle beginnings.” Hu Yin likewise said: “Those skilled in governing all under Heaven and the state simply remain watchful over subtle beginnings.” Both speak of how such beginnings must never be neglected. Zhou Dunyi pointed to their root, saying: “Being still and unmoving is sincerity; responding to a stimulus and thereupon comprehending is spiritual efficacy; movement not yet taking form, between nonbeing and being, is incipience.” In these subtle beginnings are decided, in their immediate implications, public-mindedness or selfishness, perversity or rectitude, and, in their distant consequences, decline or flourishing, survival or destruction. They cannot be left unscrutinized. Thus sincerity, spiritual efficacy, and discernment of incipience constitute sagehood.
I wish that Your Majesty, within the secluded depths of the palace, when your mind and vital energies are clear and bright, would investigate the finest distinction between principle and desire, testing it against the mirror of successes and failures past and present. “Even where nothing is visible, be as though in the presence of a superior”; “preserve this without weariness.” Exalt reverence and awe; guard against indolence and desire. Let sincerity and simplicity issue from within, and frugality and plainness be rooted in your innate nature. Proceeding from this to follow established models, you can extend the models of the sages of old; proceeding from this to guide the people, you can win the trust of even the most ignorant. All the means of allowing the people respite and recovery, so as to bring to fulfillment an achievement of utmost breadth, depth, loftiness, and illumination, can then readily be set in motion through this mind, without difficulty. In my foolishness, I cannot contain my utmost earnest devotion. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.
